fields.title: Genesis
fields.subtitle: Bereshit, “In the beginning”
fields.description: The first book of the Bible, called in Hebrew Bereshit from its opening words, “In the beginning”. It begins with God speaking light into darkness and a world he calls very good, and ends with a coffin in Egypt and a promise still waiting to be kept. Between the two: Adam and Eve in the garden and outside it, Cain and Abel, Noah and the rainbow, the tower of Babel, and then one family called out of the nations for the sake of them all — Abraham counting the stars, Isaac on the mountain, Jacob wrestling through the night, and Joseph forgiving the brothers who sold him. In the Open Word Bible, a new translation from the Hebrew given freely to the public domain, with an introduction to the book’s shape and meaning and a conclusion on where to read next.

qa.question: What is the book of Genesis?
qa.answer: The first book of the Bible and of the five books of Moses, the Torah. Its Hebrew name, Bereshit, is its first word, “In the beginning”; the name Genesis, Greek for “origin”, comes from the ancient Greek translation. Its fifty chapters run from the creation of the world to the death of Joseph in Egypt: chapters 1–11 tell of the beginnings of the world and of all peoples, and chapters 12–50 follow one family, Abraham, Isaac, Jacob and Jacob’s twelve sons, through whom God promises to bless all the families of the earth (12:3).

qa.question: Who wrote the book of Genesis?
qa.answer: Genesis does not name its author. Jewish and Christian tradition has long received it as the first of the five books of Moses, and the New Testament speaks of the Law as coming through Moses. Many scholars think the book drew on older sources and family records and reached its final form over a long period, some placing that well after Moses. Christians hold a range of views on how the book was composed, while agreeing that it is Scripture and the foundation of everything the rest of the Bible says about God, humanity and the promise.

qa.question: How is the book of Genesis structured?
qa.answer: By a heading that recurs through the book, in Hebrew “these are the toledot of…”, traditionally translated “these are the generations of”. It appears ten times (eleven, counting the repeat at 36:9), introducing the accounts of the heavens and the earth (2:4), Adam (5:1), Noah (6:9), Noah’s sons (10:1), Shem (11:10), Terah (11:27), Ishmael (25:12), Isaac (25:19), Esau (36:1 and 36:9) and Jacob (37:2). Each heading names a father and goes on to tell what came of his line, so Terah’s account is the story of Abraham, Isaac’s is the story of Jacob, and Jacob’s is the story of Joseph and his brothers.

qa.question: Does Genesis conflict with science?
qa.answer: Christians answer this in different ways. Some read the six days of Genesis 1 as ordinary days and the earth as young; others read them as long ages, or as a literary frame in which the days arrange God’s work rather than time it, or as an ancient account written to show who made the world and why, not how or when. What the chapter itself insists on is not in dispute among them: that one God made everything that exists, that he made it good, that he made human beings in his image, and that the world is his and not a god in its own right. Many believing scientists and theologians across the centuries have found no final conflict between that confession and the study of nature.

qa.question: What is God’s covenant with Abraham?
qa.answer: God’s promise, first given in Genesis 12:1–3 and confirmed by covenant in chapters 15 and 17, to make Abraham a great nation, to give his descendants the land of Canaan, to be their God, and through him to bless all the families of the earth. Abraham was old and his wife Sarah was barren, and he “put his trust in the LORD, and the LORD counted it to his credit as righteousness” (15:6). The apostle Paul reads that verse as the pattern of faith for everyone, and the promise of blessing for all nations as the gospel announced ahead of time, fulfilled in Christ (Galatians 3:8, 3:29).

qa.answer: The Open Word Bible, a new translation made directly from the Hebrew and dedicated to the public domain, printed here at its Balanced level, which aims to be accurate and to read naturally aloud. fields.title: Introduction
fields.body_html:
In the beginning God created the heavens and the earth.

— Genesis 1:1

The Bible begins where everything begins. In Hebrew this book is called Bereshit, after its first word, which means “In the beginning”. The name we use, Genesis, comes from the ancient Greek translation and means “origin”. Both are fitting. Genesis tells of the beginning of the world, of the human race, of sin and death, of nations, and of the people of Israel. And it tells of the beginning of a promise that the rest of the Bible spends itself keeping.

It opens with God and nothing else. There is no argument for his existence, no account of where he came from, no rival for him to defeat. Before Genesis tells us anything about ourselves, it tells us whose world this is.

And it ends, fifty chapters later, in a very different place: with Joseph dying in Egypt, far from the land his family had been promised, asking his brothers to carry his bones home when God comes to help them. The book that began with “Let there be light” closes with a coffin. Between those two ends lies one of the great stories ever told, and one of the most honest.

Two halves

Genesis falls into two parts of very different pace. The first, chapters 1–11, covers an enormous sweep of time in a few pages: creation, the garden, the first murder, long lists of generations, the flood, the scattering of the nations at Babel. Its subject is the whole human race.

Then, at the end of chapter 11, the camera stops and turns to one family. A man named Terah sets out from Ur of the Chaldeans with his son Abram and his daughter-in-law Sarai, of whom we are told only this: “Now Sarai was barren; she had no children.” From chapter 12 to chapter 50 the book slows almost to walking pace. It follows four generations of this one family: Abraham, Isaac, Jacob and Jacob’s twelve sons.

The change is the point. The first half shows a world that has gone wrong. The second shows what God begins to do about it. And he begins, strangely, not with an empire or an army but with an elderly couple who cannot have children.

“This is the story of…”

Genesis has its own table of contents, woven into the text. Ten headings, eleven times counting the repeat at 36:9, read in Hebrew “these are the toledot of…”, a word older translations rendered “generations”. It means something like “what came from”: a person’s descendants, and the story of what became of them. This translation renders it naturally in each place, “This is the story of…” or “This is the account of…”, but the pattern is there to be found:

  • the heavens and the earth (2:4)
  • Adam (5:1)
  • Noah (6:9)
  • the sons of Noah (10:1)
  • Shem (11:10)
  • Terah (11:27)
  • Ishmael (25:12)
  • Isaac (25:19)
  • Esau (36:1, and again at 36:9)
  • Jacob (37:2)

Two things are worth noticing. First, each heading names a father but tells the story of his children. The account of Terah is the story of Abraham; the account of Isaac is the story of Jacob and Esau; the account of Jacob is the story of Joseph and his brothers. Genesis is always looking at what comes next.

Second, the headings narrow. Again and again the book briefly lists a branch of the family that will not carry the promise (Ishmael’s, Esau’s) and then sets it aside to follow the one that will. The lists of names that tempt readers to skip are doing real work: they show a God steering, through all the branching of the human family, toward a single promise.

Creation and the image of God

The first chapter is built like a piece of music. Day by day God speaks, and it is so; he names what he has made; he sees that it is good; and a refrain closes each movement: “Evening came, and then morning.” The first three days make spaces, and the next three fill them. On the seventh day God rests, and blesses the day, and sets it apart as holy.

At the climax of the sixth day the rhythm changes. Instead of “Let there be”, God says “Let us make”, and makes human beings:

So God created human beings in his image. In the image of God he created them; male and female he created them.

— Genesis 1:27

In the ancient world, kings set up images of themselves in the lands they ruled, to show whose those lands were. Genesis says that God has already placed his image in the world, and it is every human being, man and woman alike. That is why, after the flood, the taking of a human life is forbidden “for God made human beings in his own image”.

Chapter 2 tells the story again from closer up. The LORD God shapes the man out of “dust from the ground” and breathes into him “the breath of life”; he puts him in a garden “to work it and take care of it”; he says, for the first time, that something is “not good”, the man being on his own, and makes the woman. Human beings are made of dust and made in God’s image, and Genesis never lets us forget either half. At the end of the sixth day, God looks at everything he has made, “and it was very good indeed.”

The fall and the spread of sin

Chapter 3 begins with a question: “Did God really tell you not to eat from any tree in the garden?” The serpent twists what God said, then contradicts it outright: “You certainly will not die.” The temptation is to be “like God, knowing good and evil”, to decide for oneself what good is. The woman eats, and gives some to her husband, “who was with her”, and he eats.

Their eyes are opened, and what they see is their own nakedness. They hide. And the first words God speaks to fallen humanity are not a sentence of judgement but a question:

But the LORD God called to the man, “Where are you?”

— Genesis 3:9

The man blames the woman, and God for giving her to him; the woman blames the serpent. Judgement comes: pain, sweat, and the return to dust. But inside the judgement there is a promise. God tells the serpent that the woman’s offspring will strike its head, though it will strike his heel (3:15). Christians since Irenaeus in the second century have read this as the first gospel: a descendant of Eve who would undo what the serpent had done, at cost to himself. And before God sends the man and woman out of the garden, he makes them “garments of skin” and clothes them. Even in exile, they are not left uncovered.

Then sin spreads, with grim speed. Cain is warned that “sin is crouching at your door”, and he kills his brother anyway. Asked “Where is your brother Abel?”, he answers, “Am I my brother’s keeper?” Chapter 5 lists the generations from Adam to Noah, and its refrain tolls like a bell: “and then he died”. Only once is it broken: “Enoch walked with God, and then he was no more, because God took him away.” By chapter 6 the LORD sees that every inclination of the human heart is “only evil all the time”, and his heart is deeply troubled.

Noah and the covenant

Into that darkness comes a single sentence: “But Noah found favor with the LORD.” The flood story is told with a careful symmetry, the waters rising and falling, and its turning point is a sentence that echoes through the Bible: “But God remembered Noah.” The waters go down, and Noah’s first act on dry ground is to build an altar.

God resolves that as long as the earth lasts, seedtime and harvest, summer and winter, day and night will not cease (8:22). Then he makes a covenant, not only with Noah but with every living creature: never again will a flood destroy the earth. And God gives a sign:

I have set my bow in the clouds, and it will be the sign of the covenant between me and the earth.

— Genesis 9:13

The word is the one used for a warrior’s bow, and many readers have seen in it a weapon of war hung up in the sky. But Genesis is too honest to pretend that the flood has cured the human heart. A few verses later Noah, the righteous man, lies drunk and uncovered in his tent. The waters have washed the world. They have not washed us.

Babel

The first half of the book ends with the human race united, speaking one language, and deciding to build:

Then they said, “Come, let us build ourselves a city, with a tower that reaches to the heavens, so that we may make a name for ourselves and not be scattered over the face of the whole earth.”

— Genesis 11:4

It is a project of fear as much as pride. God comes down to see their tower, which is the Bible’s gentle joke about how high it really reached, confuses their language, and scatters them anyway. The city is called Babel, which sounds in Hebrew like the word for confusion.

Read the next chapter beside this one. The builders wanted to make a name for themselves; God promises Abram that he will “make your name great”. The builders feared being scattered; God promises that through Abram “all the families of the earth will be blessed.” What human beings tried to seize, God means to give.

Abraham: called, and counted righteous

The second half of Genesis begins with a call and a promise:

Now the LORD said to Abram, “Leave your country, your relatives and your father’s household, and go to the land I will show you. I will make a great nation of you. I will bless you and make your name great, so that you will be a blessing. I will bless those who bless you, and whoever treats you with contempt I will curse; and all the families of the earth will be blessed through you.”

— Genesis 12:1–3

Everything else in the Bible can be read as the working out of those three verses. And the next verse is just as important: “Abram set out as the LORD had told him.” He was seventy-five, with a wife who could not have children and a promise of a great nation.

Genesis does not make Abraham a plaster saint. In a famine he goes down to Egypt and, afraid for his life, passes Sarai off as his sister. Later, when the promised child has not come, he and Sarai try to bring the promise about themselves through her servant Hagar, and the household is torn by it. But in chapter 15, when Abram complains that he is still childless, God takes him outside and tells him to count the stars, if he can. “Your descendants will be like that.” Then comes one of the most important sentences in Scripture:

Abram put his trust in the LORD, and the LORD counted it to his credit as righteousness.

— Genesis 15:6

Abram has done nothing yet but believe. He has not been circumcised; the law of Moses is centuries away. The apostle Paul builds his letters to the Romans and the Galatians on this verse: God counts as righteous the one who trusts him, and Abraham is the father of everyone who believes.

God renames him Abraham, “a father of many nations”. Sarah laughs to hear she will bear a son in her old age, and is answered with a question: “Is anything too wonderful for the LORD?” Isaac is born, and his name means “he laughs”. Then, in chapter 22, comes the hardest test in the book: God tells Abraham to take “your son, your only son, the one you love, Isaac” and offer him on a mountain in Moriah. On the way up, the boy asks where the lamb is:

Abraham answered, “God will see to the lamb for his burnt offering, my son.” And the two of them walked on together.

— Genesis 22:8

God stops Abraham’s hand and provides a ram, and Abraham names the place “The LORD Will See to It.” Christians have never been able to read this chapter without thinking of another Father, another only Son, and another hill, where God himself saw to the lamb.

Isaac, Jacob and the God of the unlikely

Isaac is the quietest of the patriarchs, and the promise passes through him to his twin sons, Esau and Jacob. Before they are born, their mother is told that “the elder will be servant to the younger”. It is a pattern Genesis repeats too often to be an accident: Abel over Cain, Isaac over Ishmael, Jacob over Esau, Joseph over his older brothers, Ephraim over Manasseh. God’s promises do not run along the lines of human advantage.

Jacob’s name sounds like “he grasps the heel”, and he lives up to it. He bargains away his brother’s birthright and deceives his blind father to steal his brother’s blessing, then flees for his life. And it is on the run, sleeping on the ground, that God meets him in a dream of a stairway reaching to the sky, with angels going up and down on it, and says, “I am with you.” Jacob wakes and says what many have said since in the low places of their lives: “The LORD is truly here in this place, and I had no idea!”

Twenty years later, returning home to face the brother he wronged, Jacob spends a night alone by the river Jabbok, and a man wrestles with him until dawn. Jacob will not let go: “I will not let you go unless you bless me.” He comes away limping, and with a new name:

He said, “You will be called Jacob no longer. Your name is Israel, for you have contended with God and with people and have come through victorious.”

— Genesis 32:28

He calls the place Peniel, “the face of God”, because “I have seen God face to face”. The next morning Esau, whom he had dreaded, runs to meet him, and they weep together. The grasper has learned that what he wanted most had to be received as a gift.

Joseph: “Good was what God planned”

The last and longest story in Genesis belongs to Joseph, Jacob’s favourite son, the boy with the long-sleeved robe and the dreams. His brothers sell him to traders bound for Egypt. There he is a slave, then falsely accused and imprisoned, then forgotten. Yet the narrator keeps saying one quiet thing: “The LORD was with Joseph.” In the end he is set over all Egypt, and saves the land, and his own starving family, from famine.

The story is also about the brothers. When they come to buy grain, Joseph tests whether the men who sold one brother will abandon another. And Judah, who once proposed selling Joseph, now offers himself as a slave in place of the youngest, Benjamin. Then Joseph can hold back no longer: “I am Joseph!” He tells his terrified brothers not to be angry with themselves, because “It was God who sent me on ahead of you, to keep people alive.”

After their father dies, the brothers fear that Joseph will take his revenge at last. He weeps, and answers them with the sentence that sums up the whole book:

Evil was what you planned against me; good was what God planned by it, so as to bring about what you see today: the lives of a great many people saved.

— Genesis 50:20

Joseph does not pretend the evil was not evil. He says that God was at work in it and through it, toward a good the brothers never intended, and that this leaves no room for revenge: “Do I stand in the place of God?” It is one of the deepest things the Bible says about suffering.

How to read Genesis

Genesis is a long book, but it is made almost entirely of stories, and it reads quickly. It is worth reading once straight through to feel its shape: the world (1–11), Abraham (12–25), Jacob (25–36), and Joseph (37–50).

The book does not name its author. Tradition, Jewish and Christian, has received it as the first of the five books of Moses; many scholars think it drew on older sources and took its final form over a long period. Christians hold a range of views on how it came together, but agree that it belongs at the head of the Scriptures.

Readers also ask how the first chapters relate to what the sciences say about the age of the world, and faithful Christians answer differently: some read the six days as ordinary days, others as long ages, others as a frame that arranges God’s work into a week to show its order and goal. All of them agree on what the chapter is most concerned to say: that there is one God, that the sun and moon and sea are not gods but his creatures, that the world he made is good, and that human beings bear his image. Whatever else it is, Genesis 1 is a declaration of who is Lord.

As you read, watch for the patterns: barren women who become mothers, younger sons chosen over older, promises delayed for years, altars built at every turning point, names given and changed. Notice how honestly the book tells its heroes’ failures. And listen to the questions God asks, because they are asked of the reader too. “Where are you?” “Where is your brother Abel?” “Is anything too wonderful for the LORD?”

About this translation

The text in this edition is the Open Word Bible, a new translation made directly from the Hebrew and given freely to the public domain. It is printed here at its Balanced level, which aims to be accurate and to read naturally aloud. Two of its choices in Genesis are worth knowing about before you begin.

“The LORD.” Where the Hebrew uses God’s personal name, the four letters often written Yahweh, this translation follows long Jewish and Christian custom and writes “the LORD”. Where it uses the ordinary word for God, it writes “God”. Genesis 2 joins the two for the first time: “the LORD God”.

Human beings. In chapter 1 the Hebrew word adam means humankind, “male and female”, and is translated “human beings”. Only gradually does it become the name of the first man. The word is close to adamah, “ground”, from whose dust the man is shaped.

For the reasoning behind every sentence of the translation, with the Hebrew beside it, see the Open Word Bible itself at openwordbible.org.

fields.title: Genesis 1
fields.body_html:
God creates the heavens and the earth

In the beginning God created the heavens and the earth. The earth was without form and empty. Darkness lay over the surface of the deep, while the Spirit of God hovered above the waters. God said, “Let there be light,” and light came into being. God saw that the light was good, and God divided the light from the darkness. God named the light Day, and the darkness he named Night. Evening came, and then morning: the first day.

God said, “Let there be a vault in the middle of the waters, to divide water from water.” So God made the vault and divided the waters beneath it from the waters above it. And so it happened. God named the vault Sky. Evening came, and then morning: the second day.

Then God said, “Let the waters below the sky come together into one place, and let dry land be seen.” And so it happened. God named the dry land Earth, and the gathered waters he named Seas. And God saw that it was good. Then God said, “Let the earth put forth green growth: plants that produce seed, and trees on the earth that bear fruit with its seed inside, each according to its kind.” And so it happened. The earth brought forth green growth: plants that produce seed, each according to its kind, and trees that bear fruit with its seed inside, each according to its kind. And God saw that it was good. Evening came, and then morning: the third day.

Then God said, “Let there be lights in the vault of the sky to divide the day from the night. Let them be signs that mark the appointed times, the days and the years, and let them shine in the vault of the sky to give light to the earth.” And so it happened. God made the two great lights, the larger to rule the day and the smaller to rule the night. And he made the stars. God placed them in the vault of the sky to give light to the earth, to rule over the day and the night, and to divide the light from the darkness. And God saw that it was good. Evening came, and then morning: the fourth day.

Then God said, “Let the waters teem with swarms of living creatures, and let birds fly above the earth across the vault of the sky.” So God created the great sea creatures and every kind of living thing that moves and teems in the waters, and every kind of winged bird. And God saw that it was good. God blessed them, saying, “Be fruitful and multiply, and fill the waters of the seas; and let the birds multiply across the earth.” Evening came, and then morning: the fifth day.

Living creatures and human beings

Then God said, “Let the earth bring forth living creatures, each according to its kind: livestock, creatures that move along the ground, and wild animals, each according to its kind.” And so it happened. God made the wild animals, each according to its kind, the livestock according to their kinds, and every creature that moves along the ground according to its kind. And God saw that it was good. Then God said, “Let us make human beings in our image, to be like us. Let them rule over the fish in the sea and the birds in the sky, over the livestock and all the earth, and over every creature that moves along the ground.” So God created human beings in his image. In the image of God he created them; male and female he created them. God blessed them and said to them, “Be fruitful and multiply. Fill the earth and subdue it. Rule over the fish in the sea, the birds in the sky, and every living creature that moves along the ground.” God said, “Here, I am giving you every plant that bears seed on the face of the whole earth, and every tree with seed in its fruit. They will be your food, and for every wild animal, every bird in the sky and every creature moving on the ground, for all that has life in it, the green plants will be food.” And so it happened. God looked at everything he had made, and it was very good indeed. Evening came, and then morning: the sixth day.

fields.title: Genesis 2
fields.body_html:
The seventh day

So the heavens and the earth were completed, with everything in them. On the seventh day God brought to an end the work he had been doing, and on the seventh day he stopped all the work he had done. God blessed the seventh day and set it apart as holy, since on that day he rested from all his work, all that God had created and made.

The man and the woman in the garden of Eden

This is the story of the heavens and the earth as they were created. When the LORD God made earth and heavens, no shrub of the field had yet appeared on the earth, and no plant of the field had yet sprung up, because the LORD God had not sent rain on the earth, and there was no one to work the ground. Instead, water would well up from the earth and soak the whole surface of the ground. Then the LORD God shaped the man out of dust from the ground. He breathed the breath of life into his nostrils, and the man became a living being. The LORD God planted a garden in Eden, toward the east, and there he placed the man he had shaped. Out of the ground the LORD God made every tree grow that is pleasing to look at and good for food. In the middle of the garden were the tree of life and the tree of the knowledge of good and evil. A river flowed out of Eden to water the garden, and from there it split into four branches. The first is named Pishon. It winds through the whole land of Havilah, where there is gold. The gold of that land is good, and aromatic resin and onyx stone are found there as well. The second river is named Gihon. It winds through the whole land of Cush. The third river is named Tigris. It runs east of Assyria. And the fourth river is the Euphrates. The LORD God took the man and settled him in the garden of Eden to work it and take care of it. The LORD God commanded the man, “You may eat as much as you like from any tree in the garden, but you must not eat from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, because on the day you eat from it, you will surely die.” Then the LORD God said, “It is not good for the man to be on his own. I will make him a helper who matches him.” So the LORD God formed out of the ground every wild animal and every bird of the sky, and brought them to the man to see what he would name them. Whatever the man called each living creature, that became its name. The man gave names to all the livestock, the birds of the sky and every wild animal. But no helper who matched him was found for the man. So the LORD God made the man fall into a deep sleep, and while he slept, he took one of his ribs and closed up the flesh in its place. Then the LORD God built a woman out of the rib he had taken from the man, and brought her to him. The man said, “At last, here is bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh! She will be called Woman, because she was taken out of Man.” This is why a man leaves his father and mother and clings to his wife, and they become one flesh. Both of them, the man and his wife, were naked, yet they were not ashamed.

fields.title: Genesis 3
fields.body_html:
The serpent and the forbidden tree

Now the serpent was more cunning than any wild animal the LORD God had made. It said to the woman, “Did God really tell you not to eat from any tree in the garden?” The woman answered the serpent, “We may eat fruit from the trees in the garden, but about the fruit of the tree in the middle of the garden God said, ‘You must not eat from it, and you must not touch it, or you will die.’” “You certainly will not die,” the serpent said to the woman. “God knows that when you eat from it your eyes will be opened, and you will be like God, knowing good and evil.” The woman saw that the tree was good for food, a delight to the eyes, and desirable for gaining wisdom. So she took some of its fruit and ate it. She also gave some to her husband, who was with her, and he ate it. Then the eyes of both of them were opened, and they knew that they were naked. So they sewed fig leaves together and made coverings for their waists. Then they heard the sound of the LORD God walking in the garden at the breezy time of the day, and the man and his wife hid from the LORD God among the trees of the garden. But the LORD God called to the man, “Where are you?” He answered, “I heard your sound in the garden, and I was afraid because I was naked, so I hid.” God asked, “Who told you that you were naked? Have you eaten from the tree I commanded you not to eat from?” The man said, “The woman you put here with me, she gave me fruit from the tree, and I ate it.” Then the LORD God said to the woman, “What is this that you have done?” The woman said, “The serpent tricked me, and I ate.” So the LORD God said to the serpent, “Because you have done this, you are cursed more than all the livestock and all the wild animals! You will crawl on your belly and eat dust all the days of your life. I will make you and the woman enemies, and your offspring and hers. He will strike your head, and you will strike his heel.”

To the woman he said, “I will greatly increase your pain in childbearing; with pain you will give birth to children. Your desire will be for your husband, and he will rule over you.”

To the man he said, “Because you listened to your wife and ate from the tree I commanded you not to eat from, the ground is cursed because of you. Through painful work you will eat from it all the days of your life. It will grow thorns and thistles for you, and you will eat the plants of the field. You will eat bread by the sweat of your brow until you return to the ground, because you were taken from it. You are dust, and to dust you will return.” The man named his wife Eve, because she would become the mother of all the living. And the LORD God made garments of skin for the man and his wife, and clothed them.

Sent out of the garden

Then the LORD God said, “The man has now become like one of us, knowing good and evil. He must not be allowed to reach out his hand and take from the tree of life as well, and eat, and live forever.” So the LORD God sent him out of the garden of Eden to work the ground he had been taken from. After he drove the man out, he placed cherubim on the east side of the garden of Eden, with a flaming sword that turned every way, to guard the way to the tree of life.

fields.title: Genesis 4
fields.body_html:
Cain and Abel

The man was intimate with his wife Eve, and she became pregnant and gave birth to Cain. She said, “With the help of the LORD I have brought a man into being.” Later she gave birth to his brother Abel. Abel kept flocks of sheep and goats, and Cain worked the ground. In the course of time Cain brought some of the produce of the ground as an offering to the LORD. And Abel also brought an offering: some of the firstborn of his flock, with their fat portions. The LORD looked with favor on Abel and his offering, but on Cain and his offering he did not look with favor. So Cain was very angry, and his face was downcast. Then the LORD said to Cain, “Why are you angry? Why is your face downcast? If you do what is right, will you not be accepted? But if you do not do what is right, sin is crouching at your door. It wants to have you, but you must master it.” Cain spoke to his brother Abel. And while they were in the field, Cain attacked his brother Abel and killed him. Then the LORD said to Cain, “Where is your brother Abel?” “I do not know,” he answered. “Am I my brother’s keeper?” The LORD said, “What have you done? Listen! Your brother’s blood is crying out to me from the ground. Now you are cursed, driven from the ground that opened its mouth to receive your brother’s blood from your hand. When you work the ground, it will no longer yield its crops for you. You will be a restless wanderer on the earth.” Cain said to the LORD, “My punishment is more than I can bear. Today you are driving me from the land, and I will be hidden from your presence. I will be a restless wanderer on the earth, and whoever finds me will kill me.” But the LORD said to him, “Because of this, whoever kills Cain will suffer vengeance seven times over.” Then the LORD put a mark on Cain, so that no one who found him would kill him. So Cain went out from the LORD’s presence and settled in the land of Nod, east of Eden. Cain was intimate with his wife, and she became pregnant and gave birth to Enoch. Cain was building a city, and he named it Enoch, after his son. Enoch had a son named Irad, Irad was the father of Mehujael, Mehujael was the father of Methushael, and Methushael was the father of Lamech. Lamech married two women, one named Adah and the other Zillah. Adah gave birth to Jabal. He was the father of those who live in tents and raise livestock. His brother’s name was Jubal. He was the father of all who play the lyre and the flute. Zillah also had a son, Tubal-cain, who forged all kinds of tools out of bronze and iron. Tubal-cain’s sister was Naamah. Lamech said to his wives, “Adah and Zillah, listen to me; wives of Lamech, hear my words: I have killed a man for wounding me, a young man for striking me. If Cain is avenged seven times, then Lamech seventy-seven times!” Adam was intimate with his wife again, and she gave birth to a son and named him Seth, saying, “God has given me another child in place of Abel, since Cain killed him.” Seth also had a son, and he named him Enosh. At that time people began to call on the name of the LORD.

fields.title: Genesis 5
fields.body_html:
From Adam to Noah

This is the written account of Adam’s family line. When God created human beings, he made them in the likeness of God. He created them male and female. He blessed them and named them Humankind when they were created.

When Adam had lived 130 years, he had a son in his own likeness, in his own image, and he named him Seth. After Seth was born, Adam lived 800 years and had other sons and daughters. Altogether, Adam lived 930 years, and then he died.

When Seth had lived 105 years, he became the father of Enosh. After Enosh was born, Seth lived 807 years and had other sons and daughters. Altogether, Seth lived 912 years, and then he died.

When Enosh had lived ninety years, he became the father of Kenan. After Kenan was born, Enosh lived 815 years and had other sons and daughters. Altogether, Enosh lived 905 years, and then he died.

When Kenan had lived seventy years, he became the father of Mahalalel. After Mahalalel was born, Kenan lived 840 years and had other sons and daughters. Altogether, Kenan lived 910 years, and then he died.

When Mahalalel had lived sixty-five years, he became the father of Jared. After Jared was born, Mahalalel lived 830 years and had other sons and daughters. Altogether, Mahalalel lived 895 years, and then he died.

When Jared had lived 162 years, he became the father of Enoch. After Enoch was born, Jared lived 800 years and had other sons and daughters. Altogether, Jared lived 962 years, and then he died.

When Enoch had lived sixty-five years, he became the father of Methuselah. After Methuselah was born, Enoch walked with God 300 years and had other sons and daughters. Altogether, Enoch lived 365 years. Enoch walked with God, and then he was no more, because God took him away.

When Methuselah had lived 187 years, he became the father of Lamech. After Lamech was born, Methuselah lived 782 years and had other sons and daughters. Altogether, Methuselah lived 969 years, and then he died.

When Lamech had lived 182 years, he had a son. He named him Noah, saying, “He will bring us relief from our work and from the painful toil of our hands, caused by the ground that the LORD has cursed.” After Noah was born, Lamech lived 595 years and had other sons and daughters. Altogether, Lamech lived 777 years, and then he died.

After Noah was 500 years old, he became the father of Shem, Ham and Japheth.

fields.title: Genesis 6
fields.body_html:
The sons of God and the Nephilim

When people began to increase in number on the earth and daughters were born to them, the sons of God saw that the daughters of humans were beautiful, and they married any of them they chose. Then the LORD said, “My spirit will not stay in human beings forever, for they are mortal. Their days will be 120 years.” The Nephilim were on the earth in those days, and also afterward, when the sons of God had relations with the daughters of humans and they bore them children. These were the mighty men of old, the famous men.

Evil fills the earth

The LORD saw how great the wickedness of the human race had become on the earth, and that every inclination of the thoughts of their hearts was only evil all the time. So the LORD regretted that he had made human beings on the earth, and his heart was deeply troubled. So the LORD said, “I will wipe from the face of the earth the human beings I have created, and with them the animals, the creatures that move along the ground and the birds of the sky, for I regret that I made them.” But Noah found favor with the LORD.

Noah and the ark

This is the story of Noah. Noah was a righteous man, blameless among the people of his time, and he walked with God. Noah had three sons: Shem, Ham and Japheth. Now the earth was corrupt in God’s sight and full of violence. God saw how corrupt the earth had become, for all the people on earth had corrupted their ways.

So God said to Noah, “I have decided to put an end to all people, for the earth is filled with violence because of them. I am going to destroy them along with the earth. Make yourself an ark of gopher wood. Make rooms in it, and coat it inside and out with pitch. This is how you are to make it: the ark is to be 450 feet long, 75 feet wide and 45 feet high. Make a roof for the ark and finish it to 18 inches from the top. Put a door in the side of the ark, and make it with lower, middle and upper decks. For my part, I am about to bring the flood, water over the earth, to destroy from under the sky every creature that has the breath of life in it. Everything on earth will die. But I will establish my covenant with you, and you will enter the ark: you, your sons, your wife and your sons’ wives with you. Bring into the ark two of every living creature, a male and a female, to keep them alive with you. Two of every kind of bird, of every kind of animal and of every kind of creature that moves along the ground will come to you, to be kept alive. Take with you every kind of food that is eaten and store it up, to be food for you and for them.” Noah did everything just as God commanded him.

fields.title: Genesis 7
fields.body_html:
The flood

Then the LORD said to Noah, “Go into the ark, you and all your household, for I have seen that you are righteous before me among the people of this generation. Take with you seven pairs of every kind of clean animal, a male and its mate, and one pair of every kind of animal that is not clean, a male and its mate, and seven pairs of every kind of bird of the sky, male and female, to keep their kinds alive on the face of all the earth. In seven days I will send rain on the earth for forty days and forty nights, and I will wipe from the face of the earth every living thing I have made.” Noah did everything the LORD commanded him. Noah was 600 years old when the flood waters came on the earth. And Noah and his sons and his wife and his sons’ wives went into the ark to escape the waters of the flood. Clean animals and animals that are not clean, birds and every creature that moves along the ground came to Noah in pairs and went into the ark, male and female, as God had commanded Noah. After the seven days the flood waters came on the earth. In the six hundredth year of Noah’s life, on the seventeenth day of the second month, on that very day all the springs of the great deep burst open, and the floodgates of the heavens were opened. And rain fell on the earth for forty days and forty nights. On that very day Noah and his sons, Shem, Ham and Japheth, together with his wife and the wives of his three sons, went into the ark, they and every wild animal according to its kind, all the livestock according to their kinds, every creature that moves along the ground according to its kind, and every bird according to its kind, everything with wings. They came to Noah and went into the ark in pairs, of every creature that has the breath of life. Those that went in were male and female of every creature, as God had commanded Noah. Then the LORD shut him in. For forty days the flood kept coming on the earth. The waters rose and lifted the ark, and it floated high above the earth. The waters swelled and rose higher and higher on the earth, and the ark floated on the surface of the waters. The waters rose so high on the earth that all the high mountains under the whole sky were covered. The waters rose more than 20 feet above them, and the mountains were covered. Every living creature that moved on the earth died: birds, livestock, wild animals, all the creatures that swarm over the earth, and all people. Everything on dry land that had the breath of life in its nostrils died. So every living thing on the face of the earth was wiped out, from people to animals, creatures that move along the ground and birds of the sky. They were wiped from the earth. Only Noah was left, and those with him in the ark. The waters flooded the earth for 150 days.

fields.title: Genesis 8
fields.body_html:
The waters go down

But God remembered Noah and all the wild animals and the livestock that were with him in the ark. God sent a wind over the earth, and the waters began to go down. The springs of the deep and the floodgates of the heavens were closed, and the rain stopped falling from the sky. The waters went down steadily from the earth, and at the end of the 150 days the waters had gone down. On the seventeenth day of the seventh month the ark came to rest on the mountains of Ararat. The waters went on going down until the tenth month, and on the first day of the tenth month the tops of the mountains could be seen. After forty days Noah opened the window he had made in the ark and sent out a raven. It kept flying back and forth until the waters had dried up from the earth. Then he sent out a dove to see whether the waters had gone down from the surface of the ground. But the dove found no place to set its feet, and it came back to him in the ark, for there was water over all the surface of the earth. He reached out his hand, took it and brought it back into the ark. He waited seven more days and sent out the dove from the ark again. When the dove came back to him in the evening, there in its beak was a freshly plucked olive leaf! So Noah knew that the waters had gone down from the earth. He waited seven more days and sent out the dove again, but this time it did not come back to him. By the first day of the first month of Noah’s six hundred and first year, the waters had dried up from the earth. Noah removed the covering of the ark and looked out, and the surface of the ground was dry. By the twenty-seventh day of the second month the earth was completely dry.

Out of the ark

Then God said to Noah, “Come out of the ark, you and your wife, and your sons and their wives with you. Bring out with you every living creature that is with you, the birds, the livestock and all the creatures that move along the ground, so that they can spread over the earth and be fruitful and multiply on it.” So Noah came out, together with his sons and his wife and his sons’ wives. Every animal, every creature that moves along the ground and every bird, everything that moves on the earth, came out of the ark, one kind after another. Then Noah built an altar to the LORD, and he took some of every clean animal and every clean bird and offered burnt offerings on the altar. When the LORD smelled the pleasing aroma, the LORD said in his heart, “Never again will I curse the ground because of human beings, even though every inclination of the human heart is evil from childhood. Never again will I strike down every living creature, as I have done. As long as the earth lasts, seedtime and harvest, cold and heat, summer and winter, day and night will never cease.”

fields.title: Genesis 9
fields.body_html:
God blesses Noah and his sons

Then God blessed Noah and his sons and said to them, “Be fruitful and multiply, and fill the earth. Every animal on the earth, every bird of the sky, every creature that moves along the ground and all the fish of the sea will fear you and dread you. They are placed in your power. Every living thing that moves will be food for you. Just as I gave you the green plants, I now give you everything. But you must not eat meat that still has its lifeblood in it. And for your lifeblood I will surely demand an accounting. I will demand it from every animal, and from every human being: from each person I will demand an accounting for the life of another. Whoever sheds human blood, by a human being that person’s blood will be shed; for God made human beings in his own image. As for you, be fruitful and multiply; spread over the earth and multiply on it.”

The covenant and the bow in the clouds

Then God said to Noah and to his sons with him, “I now establish my covenant with you and with your descendants after you, and with every living creature that was with you, the birds, the livestock and all the wild animals, all those that came out of the ark with you, every living creature on earth. I establish my covenant with you: never again will all life be cut off by the waters of a flood, and never again will there be a flood to destroy the earth.” And God said, “This is the sign of the covenant I am making between me and you and every living creature with you, for all generations to come: I have set my bow in the clouds, and it will be the sign of the covenant between me and the earth. Whenever I bring clouds over the earth and the bow appears in the clouds, I will remember my covenant between me and you and every living creature of every kind. Never again will the waters become a flood to destroy all life. When the bow is in the clouds, I will see it and remember the everlasting covenant between God and every living creature of every kind on the earth.” So God said to Noah, “This is the sign of the covenant I have established between me and all life on the earth.”

Noah’s sons

The sons of Noah who came out of the ark were Shem, Ham and Japheth. Ham was the father of Canaan. These three were the sons of Noah, and from them came all the people who spread over the earth. Noah, a man of the soil, was the first to plant a vineyard. When he drank some of its wine, he became drunk and lay uncovered inside his tent. Ham, the father of Canaan, saw his father naked and went out and told his two brothers. But Shem and Japheth took a garment, laid it across their shoulders and walked in backward to cover their father’s nakedness. Their faces were turned away, so they did not see their father naked. When Noah awoke from his wine and found out what his youngest son had done to him, he said, “Cursed be Canaan! He will be the lowest of servants to his brothers.” He also said, “Blessed be the LORD, the God of Shem! May Canaan be his servant. May God make room for Japheth, and may he live in the tents of Shem. May Canaan be his servant.” After the flood Noah lived 350 years. Altogether, Noah lived 950 years, and then he died.

fields.title: Genesis 10
fields.body_html:
The families of Noah’s sons

This is the account of the families of Noah’s sons, Shem, Ham and Japheth. Sons were born to them after the flood. The sons of Japheth were Gomer, Magog, Madai, Javan, Tubal, Meshech and Tiras. The sons of Gomer were Ashkenaz, Riphath and Togarmah. The sons of Javan were Elishah, Tarshish, the Kittim and the Dodanim. From these the peoples of the coasts and islands spread out into their own lands, each with its own language, by their clans and nations. The sons of Ham were Cush, Egypt, Put and Canaan. The sons of Cush were Seba, Havilah, Sabtah, Raamah and Sabteca. The sons of Raamah were Sheba and Dedan. Cush was the father of Nimrod, who became the first great warrior on the earth. He was a mighty hunter before the LORD; that is why people say, “Like Nimrod, a mighty hunter before the LORD.” His kingdom began with Babylon, Erech, Akkad and Calneh, in the land of Shinar. From that land he went to Assyria, where he built Nineveh, Rehoboth-Ir, Calah and Resen, which is between Nineveh and Calah; that is the great city. Egypt was the ancestor of the Ludites, the Anamites, the Lehabites, the Naphtuhites, the Pathrusites, the Casluhites (from whom the Philistines came) and the Caphtorites.

Canaan was the father of Sidon, his firstborn, and of Heth, and of the Jebusites, the Amorites, the Girgashites, the Hivites, the Arkites, the Sinites, the Arvadites, the Zemarites and the Hamathites. Later the clans of the Canaanites spread out, and the border of Canaan reached from Sidon toward Gerar as far as Gaza, and then toward Sodom, Gomorrah, Admah and Zeboiim, as far as Lasha. These are the descendants of Ham, by their clans and languages, in their lands and nations.

The descendants of Shem

Sons were also born to Shem, the elder brother of Japheth; Shem was the ancestor of all the sons of Eber. The sons of Shem were Elam, Asshur, Arpachshad, Lud and Aram. The sons of Aram were Uz, Hul, Gether and Mash. Arpachshad was the father of Shelah, and Shelah was the father of Eber. Two sons were born to Eber. One was named Peleg, because in his time the earth was divided. His brother was named Joktan. Joktan was the father of Almodad, Sheleph, Hazarmaveth, Jerah, Hadoram, Uzal, Diklah, Obal, Abimael, Sheba, Ophir, Havilah and Jobab. All these were sons of Joktan. The region where they lived stretched from Mesha toward Sephar, in the eastern hill country. These are the descendants of Shem, by their clans and languages, in their lands and nations. These are the clans of Noah’s sons, by their family lines, in their nations. From these the nations spread out over the earth after the flood.

fields.title: Genesis 11
fields.body_html:
The city and tower of Babel

At that time the whole world had one language and a common vocabulary. As people moved from the east, they found a plain in the land of Shinar and settled there. They said to one another, “Come, let us make bricks and bake them hard.” They used brick instead of stone, and tar instead of mortar. Then they said, “Come, let us build ourselves a city, with a tower that reaches to the heavens, so that we may make a name for ourselves and not be scattered over the face of the whole earth.” But the LORD came down to see the city and the tower that the people were building. And the LORD said, “They are one people with one language, and this is only the start of what they will do. From now on nothing they set out to do will be out of their reach. Come, let us go down and confuse their language, so that they will not understand one another.” So the LORD scattered them from there over the face of the whole earth, and they stopped building the city. That is why it was called Babel, because there the LORD confused the language of the whole world. From there the LORD scattered them over the face of the whole earth.

From Shem to Abram

This is the account of Shem’s family line. Two years after the flood, when Shem was 100 years old, he became the father of Arpachshad. After Arpachshad was born, Shem lived 500 years and had other sons and daughters.

When Arpachshad had lived thirty-five years, he became the father of Shelah. After Shelah was born, Arpachshad lived 403 years and had other sons and daughters.

When Shelah had lived thirty years, he became the father of Eber. After Eber was born, Shelah lived 403 years and had other sons and daughters.

When Eber had lived thirty-four years, he became the father of Peleg. After Peleg was born, Eber lived 430 years and had other sons and daughters.

When Peleg had lived thirty years, he became the father of Reu. After Reu was born, Peleg lived 209 years and had other sons and daughters.

When Reu had lived thirty-two years, he became the father of Serug. After Serug was born, Reu lived 207 years and had other sons and daughters.

When Serug had lived thirty years, he became the father of Nahor. After Nahor was born, Serug lived 200 years and had other sons and daughters.

When Nahor had lived twenty-nine years, he became the father of Terah. After Terah was born, Nahor lived 119 years and had other sons and daughters.

Terah’s family

After Terah had lived seventy years, he became the father of Abram, Nahor and Haran. This is the account of Terah’s family. Terah was the father of Abram, Nahor and Haran, and Haran was the father of Lot. Haran died during the lifetime of his father Terah, in the land where he was born, in Ur of the Chaldeans. Abram and Nahor both married. Abram’s wife was named Sarai, and Nahor’s wife was Milcah, the daughter of Haran, who was the father of both Milcah and Iscah. Now Sarai was barren; she had no children. Terah took his son Abram, his grandson Lot son of Haran, and his daughter-in-law Sarai, the wife of his son Abram, and together they set out from Ur of the Chaldeans to go to the land of Canaan. But when they came to Haran, they settled there. Terah lived 205 years, and he died in Haran.

fields.title: Genesis 12
fields.body_html:
The LORD calls Abram

Now the LORD said to Abram, “Leave your country, your relatives and your father’s household, and go to the land I will show you. I will make a great nation of you. I will bless you and make your name great, so that you will be a blessing. I will bless those who bless you, and whoever treats you with contempt I will curse; and all the families of the earth will be blessed through you.” Abram set out as the LORD had told him, and Lot went with him. Abram was seventy-five when he left Haran. Abram took with him his wife Sarai, his brother’s son Lot, everything they owned and the people who had become part of their household in Haran. They set out for Canaan and reached it. Abram passed through the country as far as Shechem and the great tree of Moreh. In those days the Canaanites lived in the land. Then the LORD appeared to Abram and said, “I will give this land to your descendants.” So Abram built an altar there to the LORD, who had appeared to him. From there he moved on into the hills east of Bethel and set up his tent between Bethel on the west and Ai on the east. He built an altar to the LORD there and called on the name of the LORD. Then Abram set out and kept moving on toward the Negev.

Abram and Sarai in Egypt

But famine struck the land, so severe that Abram went down to Egypt to stay there for a time. Just before they reached Egypt, Abram said to his wife Sarai, “Listen. I know you are a beautiful woman. When the Egyptians see you, they will say, ‘She is his wife,’ and they will kill me and keep you alive. Please tell them you are my sister. Then things will go well for me because of you, and I will stay alive thanks to you.” And so it was: as soon as Abram arrived in Egypt, the Egyptians noticed how very beautiful the woman was. Pharaoh’s officials saw her too and spoke highly of her to Pharaoh, and she was taken into his palace. Because of her, Pharaoh was generous to Abram, who came to own sheep, cattle and donkeys, male and female servants, she-donkeys and camels. But the LORD struck Pharaoh and his household with severe plagues because of Abram’s wife Sarai. Pharaoh called for Abram and said, “What is this you have done to me? Why did you not tell me she was your wife? Why did you claim she was your sister, and let me take her as my wife? Here she is. Take your wife and go!” Pharaoh put men in charge of Abram, and they escorted him out of the country with his wife and all his possessions.

fields.title: Genesis 13
fields.body_html:
Abram and Lot part ways

Abram left Egypt and went up to the Negev, taking his wife and all his possessions, and Lot came too. By now Abram was a very rich man, with herds and flocks, silver and gold. From the Negev he traveled in stages back to Bethel, to the spot between Bethel and Ai where he had first pitched his tent, where he had built the altar before. There Abram called on the name of the LORD. Lot, traveling with Abram, had his own flocks and herds and tents as well. The land could not sustain both of them living side by side; they had so much that they could not stay together. Before long Abram’s herdsmen and Lot’s herdsmen were at odds with each other. At that time the Canaanites and the Perizzites were also settled in the land. So Abram said to Lot, “There should be no quarrel between us, or between your herdsmen and mine. We are family. The whole land is open to you. Let us go our separate ways. You take the left and I will take the right, or you take the right and I will take the left.” Lot looked out over the Jordan plain and saw water everywhere, all the way to Zoar, as in the garden of the LORD or the land of Egypt. (That was before the LORD destroyed Sodom and Gomorrah.) So Lot chose the whole Jordan plain for himself and moved off to the east. The two of them parted. Abram remained in Canaan; Lot settled among the towns of the plain and moved his camp as far as Sodom. The people of Sodom, however, were evil and grievous sinners against the LORD. After Lot had gone, the LORD said to Abram, “Raise your eyes and look out from where you stand, to the north and south, east and west. I am giving you all the land you can see, to you and your descendants for all time. I will make your descendants as countless as the dust of the earth; only if someone could count the dust could your descendants be counted. Go and travel the land from end to end and side to side, because I am giving it to you.” So Abram moved his tents and went to live near the great trees of Mamre at Hebron, where he built an altar to the LORD.

fields.title: Genesis 14
fields.body_html:
Abram rescues Lot, and Melchizedek blesses him

In the days when Amraphel was king of Shinar, Arioch king of Ellasar, Kedorlaomer king of Elam and Tidal king of Goyim, these kings went to war against Bera king of Sodom, Birsha king of Gomorrah, Shinab king of Admah, Shemeber king of Zeboiim and the king of Bela (that is, Zoar). All these kings joined forces in the Valley of Siddim, where the Dead Sea is now. They had paid tribute to Kedorlaomer for twelve years, and in the thirteenth year they revolted. In the fourteenth year Kedorlaomer came with his allied kings and crushed the Rephaites in Ashteroth-karnaim, the Zuzites in Ham, the Emites in Shaveh-kiriathaim and the Horites in their hill country of Seir, as far as El-paran on the edge of the desert. Then they turned back and came to En-mishpat (that is, Kadesh), and they conquered the whole territory of the Amalekites, as well as the Amorites living in Hazazon-tamar. Then the kings of Sodom, Gomorrah, Admah, Zeboiim and Bela (that is, Zoar) marched out and took up battle positions in the Valley of Siddim against Kedorlaomer king of Elam, Tidal king of Goyim, Amraphel king of Shinar and Arioch king of Ellasar: four kings against five. The Valley of Siddim was riddled with tar pits. As the kings of Sodom and Gomorrah ran, some of their men fell into them, and the survivors escaped into the hills. The victors carried off everything from Sodom and Gomorrah, all their goods and food, and went on their way. Among the captives was Lot, Abram’s nephew, who lived in Sodom; they took him and all he had. Someone who escaped brought the news to Abram the Hebrew. Abram was camped by the great trees belonging to Mamre the Amorite, whose brothers were Eshcol and Aner; all three were bound by treaty to Abram. As soon as Abram learned that his kinsman was a prisoner, he mustered the 318 trained men of his household, all born in his camp, and chased the enemy as far as Dan. He split his men into groups and fell on the enemy by night. He routed them and pursued them as far as Hobah, north of Damascus. He got back all the plunder, and he brought back Lot his kinsman with his goods, as well as the women and the rest of the captives. When Abram came back from his victory over Kedorlaomer and the kings with him, the king of Sodom went out to meet him in the Valley of Shaveh, which is the King’s Valley. Then Melchizedek king of Salem brought out bread and wine. He was priest of God Most High. He blessed Abram and said, “May Abram be blessed by God Most High, Creator of heaven and earth. And blessed be God Most High, who has given your enemies into your power.” Then Abram gave him a tenth of everything. Then the king of Sodom said to Abram, “Let me have the people; you keep the goods.” Abram answered the king of Sodom, “I have lifted my hand in an oath to the LORD, God Most High, Creator of heaven and earth, that I will not keep a single thing of yours, not a thread, not a sandal strap. You will never be able to say, ‘I made Abram rich.’ I will take nothing except what my young men have already eaten. But Aner, Eshcol and Mamre, who went with me, must have their share.”

fields.title: Genesis 15
fields.body_html:
The LORD makes a covenant with Abram

Some time later the word of the LORD came to Abram in a vision: “Do not be afraid, Abram. I am your shield, and your reward will be very great.” But Abram answered, “Lord GOD, what will you give me? I am still childless, and everything I have will go to Eliezer of Damascus.” Abram went on, “Since you have not given me a child, someone born in my household will inherit from me.” Then the word of the LORD came to him: “No, he will not inherit from you. Your heir will be your own son, born of your own body.” He led Abram outside and said, “Look up into the sky and try counting the stars, if you can.” Then he told him, “Your descendants will be like that.” Abram put his trust in the LORD, and the LORD counted it to his credit as righteousness. He also told him, “I am the LORD. I brought you out of Ur of the Chaldeans to give you this land to be your own.” But Abram said, “Lord GOD, how can I be sure that I will possess it?” He answered, “Bring me a three-year-old heifer, a three-year-old female goat and a three-year-old ram, with a turtledove and a young pigeon.” Abram brought them all, split each one down the middle and laid the halves facing each other, but he did not split the birds. When birds of prey swooped down on the carcasses, Abram chased them off. When the sun was going down, a deep sleep came over Abram, and with it a great and terrifying darkness. Then the LORD said to Abram, “You must understand that your descendants will be foreigners in a land that is not theirs. They will be enslaved and oppressed for 400 years. But I will bring judgment on the nation that enslaves them, and afterward they will come out with great wealth. As for you, you will join your ancestors in peace and be buried at a ripe old age. Your descendants will return here in the fourth generation, because the Amorites’ wickedness has not yet run its full course.” After sunset, in the dark, a smoking fire pot and a blazing torch passed between the halves of the animals. That day the LORD made a covenant with Abram: “I am giving this land to your descendants, from the river of Egypt to the great river Euphrates, the land of the Kenites, Kenizzites, Kadmonites, Hittites, Perizzites, Rephaites, Amorites, Canaanites, Girgashites and Jebusites.”

fields.title: Genesis 16
fields.body_html:
Hagar and Ishmael

Sarai, Abram’s wife, had still given him no children. But she owned an Egyptian servant named Hagar. Sarai said to Abram, “You see that the LORD has not let me bear children. Take my servant; it may be that through her I will have a family.” And Abram listened to Sarai. Ten years after Abram had settled in Canaan, his wife Sarai gave him Hagar, her Egyptian servant, as a wife. He slept with Hagar, and she became pregnant. Once she knew she was carrying a child, she began to look down on her mistress. Sarai said to Abram, “You are to blame for the wrong done to me! I gave my servant to you, and now that she is pregnant she holds me in contempt. The LORD be judge between you and me!” Abram answered Sarai, “She is your slave, and she is in your hands. Deal with her as you see fit.” Then Sarai treated her so harshly that she ran away. The angel of the LORD came upon her beside a spring in the desert, the spring on the road to Shur. He asked her, “Hagar, servant of Sarai, where have you come from and where are you headed?” She answered, “I am running away from Sarai, my mistress.” The angel of the LORD said to her, “Go back to your mistress and put yourself under her authority.” The angel of the LORD also said, “I will make your descendants so many that no one will be able to count them.” Then the angel of the LORD said, “You are with child, and you will have a son. Call him Ishmael, for the LORD has listened to your suffering. He will be like a wild donkey: he will raise his hand against everyone, and everyone will raise a hand against him, and he will live at odds with all his kin.” So she gave this name to the LORD who had spoken to her: “You are the God who sees me.” For she said, “Have I truly seen the One who watches over me?” That is why the well was called Beer-lahai-roi. It is still there, between Kadesh and Bered. So Hagar bore Abram a son, and Abram named the son she had borne him Ishmael. Abram was eighty-six years old when Hagar bore him Ishmael.

fields.title: Genesis 17
fields.body_html:
Circumcision, the sign of the covenant

When Abram was ninety-nine, the LORD appeared to him and said, “I am God Almighty. Live your life before me and be wholehearted, so that I may confirm my covenant between me and you and greatly increase your descendants.” Abram fell face down, and God said to him, “Here is my covenant with you, from my side: you will become the father of many nations. Your name will no longer be Abram. From now on it is Abraham, since I have made you a father of many nations. I will make you abundantly fruitful; nations will come from you, and kings will be among your descendants. I will keep my covenant with you and your descendants after you for generations to come, as an everlasting covenant: I will be your God and the God of your descendants after you. I will give you and your descendants after you all the land of Canaan, the land where you are now a foreigner, to hold for all time, and I will be their God.” God also said to Abraham, “Your part is to keep my covenant, you and your descendants after you in every generation. Here is the covenant you and your descendants are to keep with me: every male among you is to be circumcised. You are to cut away the flesh of your foreskin, and it will be the sign of the covenant between me and you. Every male among you who is eight days old must be circumcised, generation after generation, including slaves born in your household or bought with money from a foreigner who is not one of your descendants. Every one of them, whether born in your household or bought with your money, must be circumcised. So my covenant will be in your flesh, a covenant for all time. A male who is not circumcised in the flesh of his foreskin is to be cut off from his people. He has broken my covenant.”

A son promised through Sarah

God said further to Abraham, “Your wife is not to be called Sarai any more. Sarah is her name. I will bless her and give you a son through her as well. I will bless her, and nations will come from her; kings of peoples will be among her descendants.” Abraham bowed face down, but he laughed and said to himself, “Can a man a hundred years old become a father? Can Sarah have a baby at ninety?” And Abraham said to God, “Oh, let Ishmael be the one who lives in your favor!” God replied, “No. Your wife Sarah will have a son by you, and you will name him Isaac. With him I will establish my covenant, a covenant for all time with his descendants after him. I have heard your prayer for Ishmael too. I will bless him, give him many children and multiply his descendants greatly. He will be the father of twelve chieftains, and I will make a great nation of him. But it is with Isaac, the son Sarah will bear you about this time next year, that I will establish my covenant.” When God had finished speaking with Abraham, he went up and left him. Abraham did it the same day. He took his son Ishmael and every male of his household, whether born there or bought with his money, and circumcised them, as God had told him. Abraham was ninety-nine when the flesh of his foreskin was cut away, and his son Ishmael was thirteen when he was circumcised. So Abraham and Ishmael were circumcised together that very day, together with all the men of his household, the slaves born in his house and those bought from foreigners.

fields.title: Genesis 18
fields.body_html:
Three visitors, and a plea for Sodom

The LORD appeared to Abraham by the great trees of Mamre. It was the hottest part of the day, and Abraham was sitting in the doorway of his tent. He raised his eyes and saw three men standing a little way off. At the sight of them he ran from the tent door to meet them and bowed down to the ground. “My lord,” he said, “if you are pleased with me, please do not go past your servant without stopping. Let me have some water brought so you can wash your feet; then rest here in the shade of the tree. I will fetch a bite of bread so you can regain your strength before you continue your journey, now that you have come to your servant.” They replied, “Yes, do what you have offered.” Abraham hurried into the tent and said to Sarah, “Hurry! Take about 20 quarts of fine flour, knead it and make loaves.” Next he ran to the cattle, picked out a calf, young and good, and handed it to a servant, who hurried to cook it. He set before them curds and milk and the calf he had prepared, and he waited on them under the tree while they ate. They asked him, “Where is Sarah, your wife?” “Inside the tent,” he said. The visitor said, “I will come back to you when this season comes round again, and your wife Sarah will have a son.” Sarah was listening at the tent door, behind him. Both Abraham and Sarah were old, far on in years, and Sarah no longer had her monthly periods. Sarah laughed inwardly and said to herself, “Worn out as I am, with my husband old, am I to have this delight?” Then the LORD said to Abraham, “Why did Sarah laugh? Why did she say, ‘Shall I really give birth, old as I am?’ Is anything too wonderful for the LORD? At the appointed time, when the season comes round, I will come back to you, and Sarah will have a son.” Sarah denied it. “I did not laugh,” she said, because she was frightened. But he said, “You did laugh.” The men rose to go and looked down on Sodom, and Abraham went part of the way with them to send them off. Then the LORD said, “Should I keep from Abraham what I am about to do? Abraham is certain to become a great nation, strong in numbers, and in him all the nations of the earth will find blessing. I have singled him out so that he will charge his children and his family after him to walk in the way of the LORD, doing what is right and just. That is how the LORD will fulfil for Abraham what he has spoken about him.” So the LORD said, “The cry for help that rises against Sodom and Gomorrah is loud, and their sin weighs very heavy. I will go down and see for myself whether their deeds are as bad as the cry that has come to me. If not, I will know it.” The men left there and set off toward Sodom, while Abraham stayed standing in the presence of the LORD. Then Abraham stepped forward and said, “Will you really destroy the innocent along with the guilty? Suppose there are fifty innocent people in the city. Would you still sweep it away? Would you not spare it for the sake of those fifty? It is unthinkable that you would do such a thing, putting the innocent to death with the guilty and treating them alike. Surely not! Will not the Judge of all the earth do what is right?” The LORD answered, “If I find fifty innocent people within Sodom, I will spare all of it because of them.” Abraham went on, “I have dared to speak to the Lord, I who am only dust and ashes. Suppose the fifty are five short. Will you destroy the whole city because five are missing?” He said, “If I find forty-five there, I will not destroy it.” Abraham spoke to him again: “Suppose there are forty.” He replied, “Because of the forty I will not do it.” He said, “Do not be angry, Lord, if I speak again. Suppose there are thirty.” He replied, “If I find thirty there, I will not do it.” He said, “I have dared to speak to the Lord; suppose there are twenty.” He replied, “Because of the twenty I will not destroy it.” He said, “Do not be angry, Lord, and I will speak only this one time more. Suppose there are ten.” He replied, “Because of the ten I will not destroy it.” The LORD went on his way when he had finished talking with Abraham, and Abraham went back to his own place.

fields.title: Genesis 19
fields.body_html:
The destruction of Sodom and Gomorrah

It was evening when the two angels reached Sodom. Lot was sitting at the city gate, and as soon as he saw them he stood up to greet them and bowed low, his face to the ground. “Please, my lords,” he said, “come aside to your servant’s house. Wash your feet and stay the night, and you can be up early and on your way.” “No,” they answered, “we will stay out in the square tonight.” But he kept pressing them until they turned aside with him and went into his house. He prepared a meal for them and baked bread without yeast, and they ate. They had not yet gone to bed when the men of the city, the men of Sodom, closed in around the house. Young and old, every man from every part of town was there. They shouted to Lot, “Where are the men who came to stay with you tonight? Send them out to us. We mean to have sex with them.” Lot went out to them at the doorway and closed the door behind him. “My friends,” he said, “please do not commit this wicked act. Listen, I have two daughters who have never been with a man. Let me bring them out to you, and you can do with them whatever you please. But do nothing to these men, because they have come under the protection of my roof.” “Get out of the way!” they shouted. “This fellow came here as a foreigner, and now he wants to play the judge! We will do worse to you than to them.” They pushed hard against Lot and moved in to break down the door. But the two men inside reached out, pulled Lot back into the house with them and shut the door. Then they struck the men at the doorway with a blinding light, every one of them, young and old, so that they groped about in vain for the door. Then the men said to Lot, “Do you have anyone else here? Sons-in-law, sons, daughters, or anyone else in the city who belongs to you? Get them out of this place, because we are going to destroy it. The outcry against its people has grown so great before the LORD that he has sent us to destroy the city.” So Lot went out and told the men who were engaged to his daughters, “Hurry, leave this place! The LORD is going to destroy the city!” But his sons-in-law thought he was not serious. As day was breaking, the angels pressed Lot to hurry. “Up!” they said. “Take your wife and the two daughters who are here with you, or you will be swept away when the city is punished.” When he still hesitated, the men took hold of his hand and the hands of his wife and his two daughters, because the LORD had pity on him. They led him out and left him outside the city. Once they had brought them out, one of them said, “Run for your lives! Do not look behind you or stop anywhere on the plain. Flee to the hills, or you will be swept away!” But Lot said to them, “Please, my lord, not that! You have been kind to your servant and have shown me great mercy by saving my life. But I cannot get as far as the hills. The disaster will catch me before I get there, and I will die. There is a town close by that I can reach, and it is only a small one. Please let me flee there. It is so small, is it not? Then I will live.” “Very well,” he answered. “I will grant this request as well. I will not destroy the town you speak of. But hurry and get there, because I can do nothing until you arrive.” That is why the town came to be called Zoar. By the time Lot reached Zoar, the sun was up over the land. Then the LORD sent burning sulfur pouring down on Sodom and Gomorrah. It came from the LORD, out of the sky. So he overthrew those cities and the whole plain, along with everyone who lived in the cities and every plant that grew there. But Lot’s wife, who was following behind him, looked back and was turned into a pillar of salt. Early the next morning Abraham went back to the place where he had stood in the presence of the LORD. He looked down over Sodom and Gomorrah and across the whole land of the plain, and saw smoke rising from the ground like smoke from a furnace. So when God destroyed the cities of the plain, he remembered Abraham and brought Lot out of the disaster that overturned the cities where Lot had made his home. Afterward Lot left Zoar and settled in the hills with his two daughters, because he was afraid to stay in Zoar. He and his two daughters lived in a cave. One day the older daughter said to the younger, “Our father is getting old, and there is no man anywhere around to marry us and give us children, as is the custom everywhere. Come, let us give our father wine to drink and then lie with him. That way we can keep our father’s family line alive.” That night they gave their father wine to drink, and the older daughter went in and slept with him. He was not aware of her lying down or getting up. The next day the older daughter said to the younger, “Last night I slept with my father. Let us give him wine to drink again tonight, and you go in and sleep with him. Then we will both keep our father’s line alive.” So again that night they gave their father wine, and the younger daughter went and slept with him. Again he was not aware of her lying down or getting up. In this way both of Lot’s daughters became pregnant by their own father. The older daughter had a son and named him Moab. He is the ancestor of the Moabites who live today. The younger daughter also had a son, and she named him Ben-ammi. He is the ancestor of the Ammonites who live today.

fields.title: Genesis 20
fields.body_html:
Abraham and Abimelech
