Abraham set out from there toward the southern country of the Negev. He settled between Kadesh and Shur, and for a time he lived as a foreigner in Gerar. There Abraham said of his wife Sarah, “She is my sister.” So Abimelech, the king of Gerar, sent men to fetch Sarah and took her into his household. But that night God came to Abimelech in a dream. “You are as good as dead,” he told him, “because of the woman you have taken. She already has a husband.” Abimelech had not touched her. He said, “Lord, would you put to death a people who have done no wrong? It was he who told me, ‘She is my sister,’ and she herself said, ‘He is my brother.’ My heart was honest and my hands were innocent when I did this.” God answered him in the dream, “Yes, I know you acted with an honest heart, and it was I who held you back from sinning against me, and so I gave you no chance to touch her. Now give the man back his wife. He is a prophet, and he will pray for you so that you live. But if you do not return her, know for certain that death awaits you and everyone who belongs to you.” Abimelech got up at dawn, called together all his officials and repeated all of this to them, and the men were badly frightened. Then Abimelech sent for Abraham. “What have you done to us?” he said. “What wrong did I ever do you, that you should expose me and my kingdom to so great a sin? You have treated me in a way no one should ever be treated.” Abimelech pressed him: “What did you have in mind when you did this?” Abraham answered, “I told myself that nobody here feared God, and that they would kill me to get my wife. And in fact she is my sister: my father’s daughter, though she had a different mother. Then she became my wife. When God sent me wandering away from my father’s house, I asked her to prove her loyalty to me by saying, wherever we went, that I was her brother.” Then Abimelech gave Abraham sheep and cattle and servants, both men and women, and he handed his wife Sarah back to him. And Abimelech said, “My land lies open to you. Settle anywhere that pleases you.” To Sarah he said, “I have given your brother about 25 pounds of silver. Let it show everyone with you that you have done no wrong. In the eyes of all you are cleared.” Then Abraham prayed to God, and God restored Abimelech to health, and his wife and female servants too, and they were able to bear children. For on account of Abraham’s wife Sarah, the LORD had closed every womb in Abimelech’s household.

fields.title: Genesis 21
fields.body_html:
The birth of Isaac, and Hagar and Ishmael sent away

The LORD took note of Sarah as he had said he would, and the LORD carried out for Sarah what he had spoken. Sarah conceived, and when Abraham was old she gave him a son, at the set time God had told him of. Abraham gave the name Isaac to the son who had been born to him, the son Sarah bore him. Abraham circumcised his son Isaac on the eighth day after his birth, following God’s command. Abraham was 100 years old when his son Isaac was born. Sarah said, “God has given me reason to laugh, and all who hear of it will share my laughter.” She went on, “Who would have dared to tell Abraham, ‘Sarah will be nursing babies’? But now, when he is old, I have borne him a son!” The boy grew older, and Abraham celebrated the day of his weaning with a large feast. Then Sarah saw the son that Hagar the Egyptian had borne to Abraham poking fun. and she told Abraham, “Send this slave woman and her boy away! No son of this slave is going to be an heir alongside my son Isaac.” This grieved Abraham deeply, since it was his own son at stake. But God told Abraham, “Do not be troubled about the boy and your servant. Do as Sarah says, in everything. The descendants who will carry your name will come through Isaac. But I will make the slave woman’s son into a nation as well, because he too is your child.” Abraham was up at dawn. He took food and a skin of water and handed them to Hagar, setting them on her shoulder; he handed over the boy too, and sent her away. She left and wandered in the wilderness of Beersheba. Once the skin had no water left, she laid the boy down under one of the shrubs. She moved away and sat down across from him at about the distance an arrow flies. “I will not watch while the boy dies,” she said to herself. There she sat, facing him from a distance, and she wept aloud. God heard the boy’s voice, and the angel of God called to Hagar from heaven. “What is wrong, Hagar?” he said. “Do not be afraid. God has heard the boy’s voice there where he lies. Get up, raise the boy to his feet and take him firmly by the hand. I will make a great nation of him.” God opened her eyes, and there she saw a well. She went over, filled the skin and gave the boy water to drink. God stayed with the boy while he grew. He settled in the wilderness and became an expert with the bow. He made his home in the wilderness of Paran, and his mother found him a wife from Egypt.

The treaty at Beersheba

Around that time Abimelech and Phicol, the commander of his army, spoke to Abraham: “God is with you in whatever you do. So swear to me by God, here and now, that you will never play me false, nor my children, nor their descendants after them. I have kept faith with you; keep faith in the same way with me and with this land where you have made your home as a foreigner.” Abraham replied, “I give you my oath.” Abraham, however, took Abimelech to task over a well that Abimelech’s men had taken from him by force. Abimelech said, “I have no idea who did this. You never told me, and this is the first I have heard of it.” Abraham then presented Abimelech with sheep and cattle, and the two of them entered into a covenant. Then Abraham took seven young ewes from the flock and placed them to one side. Abimelech asked Abraham, “Why have you put these seven lambs off to one side?” He answered, “Take these seven lambs from me. They will stand as my proof that I am the one who dug this well.” That is why the place was named Beersheba: the two of them took an oath there. Once the covenant at Beersheba was made, Abimelech and his army commander Phicol got up and went home to the land of the Philistines. Abraham planted a tamarisk at Beersheba. There he worshiped, calling on the name of the LORD, God Everlasting. For a long time after that, Abraham lived as a resident foreigner in the land of the Philistines.

fields.title: Genesis 22
fields.body_html:
God tests Abraham

Some time after this, God put Abraham to the test. “Abraham!” he called, and Abraham answered, “Here I am.” God said, “Please take your son, your only son, the one you love, Isaac. Go to the land of Moriah, and there, on one of the mountains that I will point out to you, offer him up as a burnt offering.” Abraham was up at dawn. He saddled his donkey and took along two of his young men, and his son Isaac. After splitting wood for the burnt offering, he started out for the place God had named to him. On the third day Abraham raised his eyes and caught sight of the place far away. Then Abraham told his young men, “You wait here with the donkey. The boy and I are going on up there to worship, and afterward we will return to you.” Abraham loaded the wood for the burnt offering onto his son Isaac and carried the fire and the knife in his own hand, and the two of them walked on side by side. Isaac said to his father Abraham, “My father.” “I am here, my son,” he answered. “I see the fire and the wood,” said Isaac, “but where is the lamb to be offered?” Abraham answered, “God will see to the lamb for his burnt offering, my son.” And the two of them walked on together. They arrived at the place God had named to him. There Abraham built the altar and stacked the wood on it; then he tied up Isaac his son and placed him on the altar, above the wood. Abraham reached for the knife and took it in his hand, ready to slaughter his son. But from heaven the angel of the LORD called to him, “Abraham, Abraham!” And Abraham said, “I am here.” He said, “Keep your hand away from the boy, and do him no harm. I now know that you are one who fears God, since you have not refused me your son, your only son.” When Abraham raised his eyes, he saw a ram behind him, held fast in the brush by its horns. So he went and took the ram, and offered it up as a burnt offering in his son’s place. Abraham named that place “The LORD Will See to It.” That is why people still say today, “On the mountain of the LORD it will be seen to.” Then the angel of the LORD called out once more to Abraham from heaven, saying, “This is the word of the LORD: By myself I swear that since you have done this, and have not kept back your son, your only son, I will pour out blessing on you and multiply your descendants until they are like the stars of the sky and the sand along the seashore. Your descendants will take the gates of their enemies, and in your descendants all the nations of the earth will find blessing, because you listened to me.” Abraham rejoined his young men, and together they got up and traveled to Beersheba, where Abraham made his home.

The sons of Nahor

Some time later word came to Abraham: “Milcah also has given your brother Nahor sons: Uz the firstborn, his brother Buz, Kemuel the father of Aram, Chesed, Hazo, Pildash, Jidlaph and Bethuel.” Bethuel was the father of Rebekah. These eight were the sons Milcah bore to Nahor, Abraham’s brother. Nahor also had a secondary wife named Reumah, and she bore him Tebah, Gaham, Tahash and Maacah.

fields.title: Genesis 23
fields.body_html:
Sarah’s death and burial

Sarah lived to the age of 127; those were the years of her life. She died at Kiriath-arba, the place now called Hebron, in the land of Canaan, and Abraham went in to mourn for Sarah and weep over her. Then Abraham rose from beside his dead wife and spoke to the Hittites. “I am a foreigner living among you as a settler. Grant me a piece of land of my own for a grave here, so that I can carry my dead away and bury her.” The Hittites replied to Abraham, “Listen to us, sir. You are a mighty prince living among us. Bury your dead in the best of our tombs. Not one of us will refuse you his tomb for burying your dead.” Then Abraham stood and bowed low before the people of the land, the Hittites. He said to them, “If you are willing for me to bury my dead, then listen to me: speak on my behalf to Ephron son of Zohar, and ask him to let me have the cave of Machpelah that belongs to him, at the edge of his field. Let him sell it to me for its full price, here in your presence, as a burial place I can own.” Ephron himself was sitting there among the Hittites, and Ephron the Hittite answered Abraham so that all the Hittites who had come to the gate of his city could hear. “No, sir, listen to me. I am giving you the field, and the cave in it as well. Here, with my own people as witnesses, I make it yours. Go and bury your dead.” Abraham bowed again before the people of the land, and said to Ephron, while they all listened, “Please, if you will only hear me out: I am paying the price of the field. Accept the money from me, so that I can bury my dead there.” Ephron answered Abraham, “Sir, hear me. Land worth about 10 pounds of silver, what is that between friends like you and me? Go and bury your dead.” Abraham agreed to Ephron’s terms and weighed out for him the silver he had named in front of the Hittites: about 10 pounds of silver, by the standard weight the traders used. So Ephron’s field in Machpelah, east of Mamre, passed into Abraham’s hands: the field with its cave and every tree within its boundaries, as his purchased property, with the Hittites, all who had come to the city gate, as witnesses. After this Abraham laid his wife Sarah to rest in the cave in the field of Machpelah, east of Mamre (that is, Hebron), in the land of Canaan. So the field and its cave were transferred from the Hittites to Abraham as a burial place of his own.

fields.title: Genesis 24
fields.body_html:
A wife for Isaac

Abraham had grown old; he was far on in years, and the LORD had given him blessing in every part of his life. Abraham said to the servant who was the elder of his household and steward of all he possessed, “Place your hand under my thigh, so that I can bind you by an oath in the name of the LORD, God of heaven and God of earth. You must not get a wife for my son from the Canaanite women of the land where I am living. Instead, travel to the land I come from, to my own people, and find a wife there for my son Isaac.” The servant asked him, “Suppose the woman refuses to follow me here. Am I then to take your son back to the land you came out of?” “On no account take my son back there,” Abraham answered. The LORD, the God of heaven, took me from my father’s family and the land of my birth. He spoke to me and swore to me, ‘I will give this land to your descendants.’ He will send his angel ahead of you, and you will find a wife there for my son. If the woman refuses to come, this oath will no longer bind you. Only, my son must never be taken back there.” So the servant placed his hand under the thigh of his master Abraham and took the oath he asked for. The servant took ten camels from his master’s herd and set off, carrying with him all sorts of fine things from his master. He made the journey to Aram-naharaim, to the town where Nahor lived. He brought the camels to their knees beside the well outside the town at evening, the hour when the women went out for water. Then he prayed: “the LORD, God of my master Abraham, let things go well for me today. Show your faithful love to my master Abraham. Here I stand at the spring, while the young women of the town come out for water. I will say to one of the girls, ‘Please tip your jar so that I can have a drink.’ If she answers, ‘Drink, and I will water your camels as well,’ may she prove to be the girl you have picked out for your servant Isaac. That is how I will know that you have kept faith with my master.” The words were hardly out of his mouth when Rebekah appeared, carrying her jar on her shoulder. Her father was Bethuel, son of Milcah and of Nahor, Abraham’s brother. The girl was strikingly beautiful and a virgin, untouched by any man. Down to the spring she went, filled her jar, and climbed up again. The servant ran to meet her. “Please,” he said, “let me have a sip of water from your jar.” “Drink, sir,” she said, and at once she let her jar down onto her hands and held it for him to drink. When he had drunk enough, she said, “I will fetch water for your camels as well, until they have had all they want.” Without delay she tipped out her jar into the trough and ran back to the well, drawing water again and again until every one of his camels had drunk. The man stood gazing at her without a word, waiting to see whether the LORD had blessed his journey with success or not. Once the camels had drunk their fill, the man brought out a gold ring for her nose, about a fifth of an ounce in weight, and two bracelets of gold for her arms, weighing about 4 ounces. “Tell me, please, whose daughter you are,” he said. “And would your father’s household have space for us to stay the night?” “My father is Bethuel,” she told him, “Milcah’s son by Nahor.” “There is straw and feed in plenty at our place,” she went on, “and a place for you to sleep as well.” The man knelt low and worshiped the LORD. “May the LORD, the God of my master Abraham, be praised!” he said. “He has not stopped being kind and true to my master. The LORD has guided me on my way straight to the home of my master’s relatives.” The girl ran home and told her mother’s household everything that had happened. Rebekah’s brother, whose name was Laban, ran out to the spring to meet the man. He had seen the nose ring and the bracelets his sister was wearing, and heard her tell what the man had said to her. So out he went, and there was the man, still standing with the camels by the spring. “Come in, blessed of the LORD!” he said. “Why stay out here? The house is ready for you, and I have made room for the camels.” So the man went into the house. Laban unloaded the camels and gave them straw and feed, and brought water for him and the men with him to wash their feet. A meal was set before him, but he said, “I will not eat before I have stated my errand.” “Go ahead,” said Laban. “I am a servant of Abraham,” he began. The LORD has greatly blessed my master, and he has become a rich and powerful man. The LORD has given him flocks and herds, silver and gold, servants both male and female, camels and donkeys. Sarah, my master’s wife, gave him a son when she was already old, and my master has handed over to him everything he owns. My master put me under oath: ‘You are not to find a wife for my son among the women of the Canaanites, whose land I live in. No, you must travel to my father’s house, to my own kin, and bring back a wife for my son from there.’ ‘But suppose the woman will not follow me?’ I asked my master. He answered, ‘The LORD, in whose presence I have lived my life, will send his angel with you and give your journey success. You will get a wife for my son from my clan, from my father’s family. You will be free of the oath you swore me once you have gone to my family. Even if they refuse to give her to you, you will be free of it.’ Today, when I reached the spring, I prayed: ‘the LORD, God of my master Abraham, if you mean to prosper the errand I have come on, here I stand at the spring. Let it be like this: a young woman comes out for water, and I ask her, “Will you give me a little water from your jar to drink?” and she answers, “Drink, and I will fetch water for your camels too.” May she be the woman the LORD has marked out for my master’s son.’ Before my silent prayer was finished, out came Rebekah, her jar on her shoulder. She went down to the spring and drew water, and I asked her, ‘Please give me a drink.’ At once she lowered the jar from her shoulder. ‘Drink,’ she said, ‘and I will give your camels water as well.’ I drank, and she gave water to the camels too. I asked her whose daughter she was, and she told me, ‘Bethuel’s, the son of Nahor, whom Milcah bore to him.’ So I fitted the ring to her nose and put the bracelets on her arms. Then I knelt and worshiped the LORD. I blessed the LORD, the God of my master Abraham, for guiding me along the true road, to take my master’s kinswoman, his brother’s granddaughter, as a wife for his son. Now then, if you are willing to act in faithful kindness toward my master, tell me. If not, say so, and I will turn elsewhere, to the right hand or the left.” Laban and Bethuel replied, “This has come from the LORD. It is not for us to say anything for it or against it. Rebekah is here in front of you. Take her with you and go; she shall be your master’s son’s wife, as the LORD has declared.” At their answer, Abraham’s servant bowed low to the ground before the LORD. Next the servant brought out silver and gold ornaments and garments as gifts for Rebekah, and he presented rich gifts to her brother and her mother as well. Only then did he and his companions eat and drink, and they stayed overnight. In the morning, when they were up, he said, “Let me return to my master.” Her brother and mother, though, wanted a delay: “Let the girl stay with us some days, perhaps ten. After that she may go.” “Do not keep me waiting,” he said, “since the LORD has made my journey succeed. Let me leave and go back to my master.” “Let us call the girl,” they said, “and hear what she says.” They called Rebekah in. “Are you willing to go now with this man?” they asked. “I will go,” she answered. So they said goodbye to their sister Rebekah and her nurse, and sent them off with Abraham’s servant and his men. They gave Rebekah their blessing: “Sister, may you become the mother of countless thousands. May your descendants take the cities of their enemies.” Rebekah and her young women set out, riding on the camels behind the man. So the servant took Rebekah and began the journey home. Meanwhile Isaac had come back from Beer-lahai-roi; he was living in the Negev at the time. Toward evening Isaac had gone out into the countryside to reflect, and raising his eyes he saw camels on their way. Rebekah, for her part, raised her eyes, and at the sight of Isaac she got down quickly from the camel. “Who is that man walking through the field toward us?” she asked the servant. “It is my master,” he replied. So she drew her veil over her face. The servant reported to Isaac everything he had done. Isaac brought Rebekah into the tent that had been his mother Sarah’s. He took her as his wife, and he loved her. So Isaac was consoled for the loss of his mother.

fields.title: Genesis 25
fields.body_html:
Abraham’s last years and death

Abraham married again; his new wife’s name was Keturah. She bore him six sons: Zimran, Jokshan, Medan, Midian, Ishbak and Shuah. Jokshan was the father of Sheba and Dedan. The descendants of Dedan were the Asshurites, the Letushites and the Leummites. Midian’s sons were Ephah, Epher, Hanoch, Abida and Eldaah. All these were Keturah’s descendants. Abraham handed over all his property to Isaac. To the sons of his concubines Abraham gave gifts, and while he was still alive he sent them away east, to the eastern lands, far from his son Isaac. Abraham lived 175 years in all. Then Abraham’s breath failed and he died at a ripe old age, an old man content with his years, and he was gathered to his people. His sons Isaac and Ishmael laid him in the cave of Machpelah, east of Mamre, in the field that had belonged to Ephron son of Zohar the Hittite, which Abraham had bought from the Hittites. So Abraham and his wife Sarah were laid to rest in the same place. Once Abraham was dead, God blessed his son Isaac, and Isaac settled near Beer-lahai-roi.

The family of Ishmael

This is the account of the family of Ishmael, Abraham’s son by Hagar the Egyptian, Sarah’s servant. Here are the names of Ishmael’s sons, by name and family line: Nebaioth, Ishmael’s firstborn, then Kedar, Adbeel, Mibsam, Mishma, Dumah, Massa, Hadad, Tema, Jetur, Naphish and Kedemah. These are Ishmael’s sons, and these their names, by their villages and camps: twelve chieftains, each over his own tribe. Ishmael lived 137 years. His breath failed, he died, and he was gathered to his people. Ishmael’s people ranged from Havilah to Shur, which faces Egypt on the road toward Asshur. They made their home in defiance of all their kin.

Esau and Jacob are born

This is the account of the family of Isaac, Abraham’s son. Abraham became the father of Isaac. Isaac was forty when he took Rebekah as his wife. She was the daughter of Bethuel and the sister of Laban, Arameans of Paddan-aram. Isaac pleaded with the LORD for his wife, because she was unable to have children. The LORD granted his request, and Rebekah conceived. The children inside her crushed against each other, and she said, “If it is like this, what is happening to me?” So she went to seek an answer from the LORD. The LORD told her, “Two nations are inside you; two peoples will come from your body and go separate ways. One will be mightier than the other, and the elder will be servant to the younger.” Her days of pregnancy came to an end, and there were twins in her womb. The first one came out reddish, his whole body covered with hair like a fur cloak, and they named him Esau. Next came his brother, his hand clutching Esau’s heel, and he was named Jacob. Isaac was sixty years old at their birth. When the boys were grown, Esau was a skilled hunter, at home in the wild, but Jacob was a steady man who lived among the tents. Isaac loved Esau, since he enjoyed the meat Esau hunted, but Rebekah loved Jacob. One day Jacob had made a stew, and Esau came in from the open country, worn out. “Let me wolf down some of that red stuff, that red stuff there,” Esau said to Jacob, “I am worn out!” That is how he came to be called Edom. Jacob answered, “First sell me your rights as the firstborn, here and now.” “I am at death’s door,” Esau said. “What use is a birthright to me?” “Swear it to me here and now,” said Jacob. So Esau gave him his oath and sold his rights as the firstborn to Jacob. Then Jacob handed Esau bread and stew made of lentils. Esau ate and drank, got up and left. That was how little Esau cared for his birthright.

fields.title: Genesis 26
fields.body_html:
Isaac and Abimelech

Famine came to the land again, a second one after the famine of Abraham’s time, and Isaac went to Gerar, to Abimelech king of the Philistines. There the LORD appeared to Isaac and said, “Do not go down to Egypt. Settle in whatever land I name to you. Stay on in this land as a resident foreigner, and I will be with you and bless you. It is to you and your descendants that I will give all these territories, and I will make good the oath I swore to your father Abraham. I will make your descendants as numerous as the stars in the sky and give them all these lands, and through your descendants every nation on earth will find blessing, because Abraham did as I told him and guarded all I gave him to keep: my commands, my statutes and my teachings.” So Isaac settled in Gerar. When the local men asked about his wife, he answered, “She is my sister.” He was afraid to say she was his wife, thinking, “They might kill me here for Rebekah’s sake,” for she was a lovely woman. After Isaac had lived there for some time, Abimelech king of the Philistines happened to look down from a window, and there was Isaac, embracing his wife Rebekah. Abimelech sent for Isaac. “So she is your wife after all!” he said. “Why did you tell us she was your sister?” Isaac replied, “I was afraid someone would kill me for her.” “What a thing to do to us!” Abimelech said. “It would have taken very little for one of the people to sleep with your wife, and you would have made us all guilty.” So Abimelech warned all his people, “Whoever touches this man or his wife must die.” Isaac sowed grain in that land, and that year it gave him a hundred times as much as he sowed. The LORD blessed him. So Isaac grew great. He went on growing greater and greater until he was a man of enormous wealth. He came to own flocks and herds and a large household of servants, and the Philistines envied him. The Philistines had blocked every well that his father’s servants dug in Abraham’s lifetime, filling them in with dirt. Then Abimelech told Isaac, “Go and live somewhere away from us; you have grown much stronger than we are.” So Isaac moved away and pitched his camp in the Gerar valley, and he settled there. Isaac dug out once more the water wells from his father Abraham’s day, which the Philistines had choked up after Abraham’s death, and he called them by the same names his father had used. Isaac’s servants dug in the valley and struck a well of fresh, flowing water. But the herdsmen of Gerar argued with Isaac’s herdsmen, insisting, “This water belongs to us.” So he named the well Esek, “Dispute”, because of the dispute they had raised with him. They dug a second well, and there was a quarrel over that one too, so he named it Sitnah, “Hostility”. He moved on from there and dug yet another well, and this time no one quarreled over it. He named it Rehoboth, “Open Spaces”, saying, “Now at last the LORD has made space for us, and we will be fruitful in the land.” From there he went up to Beersheba. That night the LORD appeared to Isaac. “I am your father Abraham’s God,” he said. “You have nothing to fear, because I am with you. For the sake of Abraham my servant I will bless you and make your descendants many.” Isaac built an altar there and called on the name of the LORD. He set up his tent there, and his servants started digging a well. Then Abimelech came out from Gerar to see him, together with his counselor Ahuzzath and Phicol, his army commander. Isaac asked them, “Why have you come to me? You hated me and drove me away.” They replied, “It is plain to us that the LORD has been with you. So we thought, ‘Let the two sides, we and you, be bound by an oath.’ We want to make a covenant with you, that you will not harm us, since we did not touch you; we did you nothing but good and sent you off in peace. You are the one whom the LORD has blessed now.” Isaac prepared a banquet for them, and they ate and drank. They were up early the next morning and bound themselves by oath to each other. Isaac then sent them on their way, and they parted from him in peace. That same day Isaac’s servants came to report on the well they had been digging. “We have struck water!” they told him. He named it Shibah, “Oath”, and that is why the town is called Beersheba to this day.

Esau’s Hittite wives

At forty, Esau took two wives, both of them Hittites: Judith, daughter of Beeri, and Basemath, daughter of Elon. These wives made life bitter for Isaac and Rebekah.

fields.title: Genesis 27
fields.body_html:
Jacob takes Esau’s blessing

Isaac had grown old, and his sight had faded until he could no longer see. He sent for Esau, the older of his two sons, and said, “My son!” “Yes, I am here,” Esau answered. “I am an old man now,” Isaac said, “and any day could be my last. So take your hunting things, your quiver and your bow, and go out into the open country and bring down some wild game for me. and cook it into the savory dish I am fond of. Bring it to me to eat, so that I can give you my blessing myself before I die.” Now Rebekah had been listening while Isaac talked to their son Esau. So when Esau went off to the open country to hunt game and bring it back, Rebekah said to her son Jacob, “Listen. I overheard your father telling your brother Esau, ‘Bring me some game and make me a tasty meal. After I have eaten I will bless you in the presence of the LORD before I die.’ Now, my son, do exactly as I tell you. Go out to the flock and pick out two fine young goats for me. I will make them into the kind of savory dish your father likes. Then you take it in to your father to eat, so that it is you he blesses before he dies.” But Jacob objected to his mother Rebekah. “Esau my brother is covered with hair,” he said, “and my skin is smooth. Suppose my father touches me. He will see that I am making a fool of him, and I will bring a curse on myself instead of a blessing.” “Then let the curse be mine, my son,” his mother replied. “Just do as I say. Go and get the goats for me.” So Jacob went and got them and brought them to his mother, and she cooked a savory dish the way his father liked it. Then Rebekah took her older son Esau’s finest clothes, which she kept in the house, and dressed her younger son Jacob in them. She also covered his hands and the smooth skin of his neck with the goatskins. Then she handed her son Jacob the savory dish and the bread she had made. He went in to his father and said, “Father!” “Yes,” said Isaac. “Which of my sons are you?” “It is Esau, your firstborn,” Jacob told his father. “I have done what you asked. Please sit up and eat some of the game I caught, and then give me your blessing.” “How did you find it so fast, my son?” Isaac asked. “The LORD your God put it in my path,” he answered. Then Isaac said to Jacob, “Come closer, my son, and let me touch you, to know whether you really are my son Esau.” Jacob came close to his father Isaac, who felt him and said, “It sounds like Jacob, but these hands are Esau’s.” He did not see through it, because Jacob’s hands were hairy like his brother Esau’s, and so he blessed him. “Are you truly my son Esau?” he asked again. “I am,” said Jacob. “Then serve it to me,” Isaac said, “so that I may eat my son’s game and give you my blessing.” Jacob set the food before him, and he ate. He also brought him wine, and he drank. Then his father Isaac said to him, “Come here, my son, and kiss me.” So he came close and kissed him, and when Isaac caught the smell of his clothes, he blessed him: “Ah, my son smells like open country that the LORD has blessed! May God grant you the dew that falls from the sky and the riches of fertile soil, with grain and new wine in abundance. Let peoples be your servants and nations bow low before you. Rule over your brothers, and let your mother’s sons bow before you. Whoever curses you, let him be cursed; whoever blesses you, let him be blessed.” Isaac had just finished blessing Jacob, and Jacob had scarcely left his father’s presence, when his brother Esau came back from the hunt. He too made a savory dish and brought it to his father. “Sit up, Father,” he said, “and eat some of your son’s game, so that you can bless me.” “Who are you?” his father Isaac asked him. “Your son,” he said, “your firstborn, Esau.” Isaac began to shake all over. “Then who was it,” he said, “that hunted game and brought it to me? I ate it all before you came, and I gave him my blessing, and blessed he will remain!” When Esau heard what his father said, he let out a loud and anguished cry. “Father, bless me as well!” he begged. But Isaac said, “Your brother came here with a trick and carried off your blessing.” “No wonder he is called Jacob!” Esau said. “Twice now he has gone behind my back and cheated me. First he took my birthright, and now look, he has taken my blessing too.” Then he asked, “Is there no blessing left that you saved for me?” Isaac answered Esau, “I have already made him your master. I have given him all his relatives to serve him, and grain and new wine to keep him. So what is there left for me to do for you, my son?” “Is that the only blessing you have, Father?” Esau said. “Bless me as well, my father!” And Esau sobbed out loud. His father Isaac answered him: “Far from the rich soil of the earth you will make your home, and far from the dew of the sky above. Your sword will win you your living, and you will be your brother’s servant. Yet a day will come when you break loose and throw off the yoke he has laid on your neck.” Esau nursed a grudge against Jacob because of the blessing his father had given him. He told himself, “My father will soon be dead and mourned. When that time is over, I will kill my brother Jacob.” When Rebekah was told what her older son Esau was saying, she sent for her younger son Jacob and told him, “Your brother Esau is finding comfort in the thought of killing you. Now, my son, do as I say. Leave now and escape to my brother Laban in Haran. Live with him for a short time, until your brother’s rage has cooled, until his anger toward you has gone and he has forgotten what you did to him. Then I will send word and bring you back. Must I be robbed of you both in a single day?” Then Rebekah said to Isaac, “These Hittite women make my life a misery. If Jacob also marries one of these local Hittite women, I might as well be dead.”

fields.title: Genesis 28
fields.body_html:
Jacob sent to Paddan-aram

So Isaac sent for Jacob and blessed him, and gave him this charge: “Do not take any Canaanite woman as your wife. Set out now for Paddan-aram, to the household of your mother’s father Bethuel, and find yourself a wife there among the daughters of your uncle Laban. May God Almighty bless you, give you children and make them many, until you grow into a whole gathering of peoples. May he give you and your descendants the blessing he gave Abraham, so that you will possess the land where you now live as a foreigner, the land God gave to Abraham.” Then Isaac sent Jacob on his way, and he set out for Paddan-aram, to Laban son of Bethuel the Aramean. Laban was the brother of Rebekah, the mother of Jacob and Esau. Esau learned that Isaac had blessed Jacob and sent him to Paddan-aram to find a wife there, and that when he blessed him he had told him, “Do not marry a Canaanite woman,” and that Jacob had done what his father and mother told him and gone to Paddan-aram. It was clear to Esau, then, that his father Isaac did not approve of Canaanite women, so he went to Ishmael’s family and, besides the wives he already had, took as his wife Mahalath, the daughter of Abraham’s son Ishmael and sister of Nebaioth.

Jacob’s dream at Bethel

Jacob left Beersheba and set out for Haran. He came to a certain place and stopped there for the night, because the sun had gone down. Taking one of the stones from there, he put it by his head and lay down to sleep in that place. He dreamed, and there before him was a stairway standing on the ground, its top touching the sky, with God’s angels climbing up and coming down on it. There above it stood the LORD, and he said, “I am the LORD, the God of your father Abraham and of Isaac. To you and to your descendants I will give the ground you are lying on. Your descendants will be as countless as the dust of the earth, and you will burst out westward and eastward, northward and southward. Through you and your descendants, all the families of the earth will receive blessing. I am with you. I will guard you everywhere you go and bring you back to this land. I will not abandon you before I have done all I told you I would do.” When Jacob woke from sleep, he said, “The LORD is truly here in this place, and I had no idea!” He was filled with fear and said, “What a fearsome place this is! This is God’s own house, and here is the doorway into heaven.” Early the next morning Jacob took the stone he had placed by his head, stood it upright as a sacred pillar, and poured oil over its top. He named that place Bethel, though the town had been called Luz before. Then Jacob made a vow: “If God stays with me and protects me on the road I am traveling, and provides me with food to eat and clothes to put on, and I come back safely to my father’s house, then the LORD will be my God, and this stone I have set up as a pillar will be God’s house. And of everything you give me, I will give a tenth back to you.”

fields.title: Genesis 29
fields.body_html:
Jacob marries Leah and Rachel

Jacob went on his way and came to the land of the eastern peoples. There he saw a well out in the open country, with three flocks of sheep lying beside it, because the flocks were watered from that well. A big stone covered the opening of the well. The custom was that when all the flocks had gathered there, the shepherds would roll the stone off the well’s opening and water the sheep, and then put the stone back in place over the opening. “Friends, where are you from?” Jacob asked them. “From Haran,” they answered. “Do you know Laban, Nahor’s grandson?” he asked. “Yes, we know him,” they said. “Is he well?” he asked. “He is,” they replied, “and here comes his daughter Rachel with the sheep now.” “But it is the middle of the day,” Jacob said, “far too early to bring the animals in. Why not water the sheep and take them back to graze?” “We are not allowed to,” they answered, “until all the flocks have come in and the stone has been rolled off the well. Then we can water the sheep.” He was still talking with them when Rachel arrived with her father’s sheep, since she was the one who looked after them. When Jacob saw Rachel, the daughter of his uncle Laban, with Laban’s sheep, he stepped forward, rolled the stone off the well’s opening by himself, and watered his uncle’s flock. Then Jacob kissed Rachel and broke into loud weeping. He explained to Rachel that he was a relative of her father, Rebekah’s son, and she ran off to tell her father. As soon as Laban heard about Jacob, his sister’s son, he ran out to meet him, hugged and kissed him, and took him home. Jacob told Laban everything that had happened. “You really are my own bone and flesh!” Laban said to him. Jacob stayed on with him for a whole month. Then Laban said to Jacob, “You are my relative, but that is no reason for you to work for me without pay. Tell me what you want to be paid.” Laban had two daughters. The elder was called Leah, and the younger Rachel. Leah’s eyes were delicate, but Rachel was shapely and lovely to look at. Jacob had fallen in love with Rachel, so he said, “I will work for you seven years in return for your younger daughter Rachel.” “Better that she should go to you than to some other man,” Laban answered. “Stay here with me.” So Jacob worked seven years to win Rachel, and because he loved her so much, the years went by for him as if they were only a few days. Then Jacob said to Laban, “My time is up. Give me my wife, so that I may sleep with her.” So Laban invited all the people of the place and gave a wedding feast. But when evening came, Laban took his daughter Leah and brought her to Jacob, and Jacob slept with her. (Laban had given his servant Zilpah to his daughter Leah, to be her servant.) In the light of morning Jacob saw that it was Leah. “What have you done to me?” he said to Laban. “It was Rachel I worked for! Why have you tricked me?” “It is not our custom here,” Laban replied, “to give the younger daughter in marriage before the firstborn. Finish out this one’s wedding week, and then we will give you the other one too, in return for another seven years of work for me.” Jacob agreed, and when Leah’s week was over, Laban gave him his daughter Rachel as his wife. (Laban gave his servant Bilhah to his daughter Rachel, to be her servant.) Jacob slept with Rachel as well, and he loved Rachel more than Leah. And he worked for Laban seven more years. When the LORD saw that Leah was unloved, he let her conceive, while Rachel remained childless. Leah became pregnant and gave birth to a son. She named him Reuben, saying, “The LORD has seen how I suffer. Surely now my husband will love me.” She conceived again and had another son. “The LORD has heard that I am unloved,” she said, “and so he has given me this son as well.” So she named him Simeon. Once more she conceived and had a son. “Now at last my husband will become attached to me,” she said, “because I have given him three sons.” That is why he was named Levi. She conceived yet again and gave birth to a son. “Now I will give thanks to the LORD,” she said, and so she named him Judah. Then for a time she had no more children.

fields.title: Genesis 30
fields.body_html:
Jacob’s children, and his flocks

Rachel was bearing Jacob no children, and seeing this she grew jealous of her sister. “Give me sons,” she said to Jacob, “or I will die!” Jacob grew angry with Rachel. “Can I take the place of God?” he said. “It is God who has kept you from having children.” “Take my servant Bilhah,” she said. “Lie with her, so that she can give birth on my knees and I may gain a family through her as well.” So Rachel gave Jacob her servant Bilhah as a wife, and Jacob lay with her. Bilhah became pregnant and bore Jacob a son. Rachel said, “God has judged my case and heard my cry, and he has given me a son.” That is why she named him Dan. Rachel’s servant Bilhah became pregnant again and bore Jacob a second son. Then Rachel said, “I have fought a mighty struggle with my sister, and I have won.” So she named him Naphtali. Leah, seeing that her childbearing had come to an end, gave her servant Zilpah to Jacob as a wife. Leah’s servant Zilpah bore Jacob a son. “Fortune has come to me!” Leah said, and she named him Gad. Then Zilpah, Leah’s servant, bore Jacob a second son. Leah said, “Happy am I! Women everywhere will speak of my happiness.” So she named him Asher. At wheat harvest time Reuben was out in the fields and came upon some mandrakes, which he brought home to his mother Leah. Rachel asked Leah, “Please let me have some of the mandrakes your son found.” But Leah answered, “Is it a small thing to you that you have taken my husband? And now you would take my son’s mandrakes too?” Rachel said, “Then Jacob may sleep with you tonight; that is the price of your son’s mandrakes.” That evening, as Jacob was coming in from the fields, Leah went out to him and said, “Tonight you are coming to me. I have paid for you with my son’s mandrakes.” And he spent that night with her. God heard Leah’s prayer. She conceived and gave Jacob a fifth son. Leah said, “God has given me my wages for giving my servant to my husband.” So she named him Issachar. Once more Leah became pregnant, and she bore Jacob a sixth son. Leah said, “God has endowed me with a rich gift. Now at last my husband will honor me, since I have borne him six sons.” So she named him Zebulun. Afterward she had a daughter, whom she named Dinah. Then God remembered Rachel. He heard her prayers and opened her womb. She conceived and bore a son, and she said, “God has removed my shame.” She called him Joseph, for she said, “May the LORD add one more son to me.” After Rachel had given birth to Joseph, Jacob said to Laban, “Let me go now, so that I can return to my own home and country. Let me take my wives and my children, for whom I served you, and go. You yourself know the work I have done for you.” But Laban said to him, “If you are well disposed toward me, stay. I have learned by omens that the LORD has blessed me because of you.” He went on, “Tell me what wages you want, and I will give them.” Jacob replied, “You know what my service has been to you, and what has become of your herds while I tended them. Before I came you had only a little, and it has multiplied many times over; the LORD has blessed you with every step I took. But when am I to provide for my own family?” Laban asked, “What am I to give you?” “Nothing at all,” Jacob answered. “Just agree to one condition, and I will once again shepherd your flocks and guard them. Today I will pass through all your flocks and set apart every animal that is speckled or spotted: the dark ones among the lambs and the spotted and speckled among the goats. These will be my pay. Later on, my honesty will be my witness. Whenever you come to look over my wages, if I have any goat without speckles or spots, or any lamb that is not dark, you may count it as stolen.” Laban said, “Very well, let it be just as you say.” But on that very day Laban picked out the male goats with stripes or spots, the female goats with speckles or spots, any with white on them, and every dark lamb, and handed them over to his sons. He then moved them a three days’ journey away from Jacob, and Jacob was left to pasture the rest of Laban’s flocks. Jacob then took freshly cut sticks of poplar, almond and plane wood and peeled bark off them in strips, baring the white wood underneath. He set the peeled sticks in the troughs at the watering places, right in front of the animals as they came to drink, for they came into heat when they came to drink. The flocks bred in front of the sticks, and their young were born striped, speckled and spotted. Jacob kept the lambs apart, but turned the animals to face the striped and dark ones in Laban’s flock. In this way he built up flocks of his own, which he kept apart from Laban’s. Each time the sturdier animals were mating, Jacob laid the sticks in the troughs in full view of the flock, so that they bred among the sticks; but when the weaker animals mated, he left the sticks out. In this way the feeble animals ended up as Laban’s and the strong ones as Jacob’s. So Jacob grew richer and richer. He came to own great flocks, servants both female and male, camels and donkeys.

fields.title: Genesis 31
fields.body_html:
Jacob leaves Laban

Jacob heard what Laban’s sons were saying: “Jacob has taken everything that belonged to our father. All his riches come from our father’s property.” Jacob also saw from Laban’s face that he no longer felt as he once had toward him. The LORD said to Jacob, “Return to your fathers’ land and to your own people. I will be with you.” Jacob therefore called Rachel and Leah out to the pasture where he had his flock. He told them, “I can tell from your father’s face that he is not the same toward me as he was. But the God of my father has stood by me. You yourselves know that I have given your father my full strength in his service. Even so, your father has tricked me and altered my wages time after time. But God would not let him do me any harm. Whenever he said, ‘The speckled ones will be your pay,’ the whole flock had speckled young. And whenever he said, ‘The striped ones will be your pay,’ the whole flock bore striped young. So it is God who has taken your father’s livestock away from him and given them to me. At the season when the flocks were mating, I lifted my eyes and saw in a dream that the male goats mounting the females were striped, speckled and mottled. And the angel of God called to me in the dream, ‘Jacob!’ ‘Yes, I am here,’ I answered. He said, ‘Raise your eyes and look: every male goat mounting the flock is striped, speckled or mottled, for I have taken note of everything Laban is doing to you. I am the God of Bethel, where you poured oil on a pillar and made a vow to me. Now get up, leave this land, and go back to the land of your birth.’” Rachel and Leah replied, “Is there anything left for us to inherit from our father’s house? He treats us as outsiders. He sold us, and then he swallowed up the whole price paid for us. Whatever riches God has taken from our father are ours and our children’s by right. Now then, do everything God has said to you.” Jacob set out at once, putting his children and wives on camels, and he drove off all his herds and all the goods he had gained in Paddan-aram, the livestock that he had acquired there, to go to his father Isaac in the land of Canaan. Laban was away shearing his sheep, and Rachel took the household gods that belonged to her father. And Jacob outwitted Laban the Aramean by not letting him know that he meant to run away. He fled with all that was his. Setting out, he crossed the Euphrates and turned toward the hill country of Gilead. Three days later Laban learned that Jacob had run away. Laban took his relatives with him and went after Jacob, and after seven days’ travel he caught up with him in the hill country of Gilead. But in a dream by night God came to Laban the Aramean and warned him, “Watch yourself: do not say a word to Jacob, good or bad.” Laban caught up with Jacob, who had pitched his tent in the hills, and Laban and his relatives camped in the hill country of Gilead too. “What is this you have done?” Laban said to Jacob. “You have tricked me and driven my daughters off like prisoners taken at sword point. Why did you slip away in secret and fool me, without a word to me? I would have given you a send-off with celebrating and singing, with drums and harps. You gave me no chance to kiss my grandchildren and daughters farewell. That was a foolish thing to do. It is within my power to do you all harm, but last night the God of your father spoke to me: ‘Watch yourself: do not say a word to Jacob, good or bad.’ Now I understand you went away because you were homesick for your father’s house. But why did you steal my gods?” Jacob replied, “I was afraid. I told myself you would snatch your daughters away from me. As for your gods, whoever has them will be put to death. With our relatives as witnesses, search for anything of yours that I have, and take it.” Jacob had no idea that Rachel had stolen them. Laban searched Jacob’s tent, Leah’s tent and the tent of the two female servants, and found nothing. Coming out of Leah’s tent, he went on into Rachel’s. Rachel, though, had taken the household gods, tucked them into her camel saddle and sat down on top of them. Laban felt through the whole tent without finding them. She said to her father, “Please, my lord, do not be offended that I do not rise before you; it is my time of the month.” He went on searching, but the household gods were not to be found. Jacob became angry and argued with Laban. “What wrong have I done?” he said to him. “What is my offense, that you came after me in such hot pursuit? You have gone through every one of my things. Have you found a single thing from your house? Lay it out here before your kinsmen and mine, and they can settle the matter between us. For twenty years I was with you. Not one of your ewes or she-goats miscarried, and I never ate a ram of your flock. When a wild animal killed one, I did not bring it to you to show it was not my fault; I made up the loss myself. You made me pay for anything stolen, by day or by night. That is how it was: by day the heat wore me down, by night the cold, and I could not sleep. That was my life for twenty years in your house: fourteen years of work for your two daughters and six for your flocks, while you changed my wages again and again. Had the God of my father, the God of Abraham, the One whom Isaac fears, not stood by me, you would have sent me off with empty hands by now. But God saw how I suffered and how hard I toiled, and last night he gave his verdict.” Laban answered, “These daughters are mine, these children are mine, these flocks are mine; everything in front of you belongs to me. Yet what can I do today for my own daughters, or for the children they have had? So come, you and I will make a covenant, and it will stand as a witness between the two of us.” Jacob then took a stone and stood it upright as a pillar. He told his kinsmen to gather stones, and they brought stones and made a heap, and there beside the heap they shared a meal. Laban named it Jegar-sahadutha, and Jacob named it Galeed. “This heap stands as a witness between you and me today,” Laban said. So it was named Galeed, and also Mizpah, for he said, “Let the LORD be on watch between us when we are out of sight of each other. Should you ever mistreat my daughters or marry other women besides them, though no one else is with us, see, God is witness between you and me.” Then Laban said to Jacob, “Look at this heap, and look at the pillar I have raised between us. The heap and the pillar both bear witness: I will not cross over past this heap to attack you, and you will not cross past this heap and this pillar to attack me. Let the God of Abraham and the God of Nahor, the God of their father, judge between us.” So Jacob swore by the One his father Isaac feared. Then Jacob offered a sacrifice there on the mountain and invited his relatives to share the meal. They ate together and spent the night on the mountain. Laban rose at dawn, kissed his grandchildren and his daughters, and gave them his blessing. Then he started back to his own home.

fields.title: Genesis 32
fields.body_html:
Laban goes home, and angels meet Jacob

As Jacob continued on his journey, angels of God met him. At the sight of them Jacob said, “This is God’s own camp!” and he called the place Mahanaim.

Gifts for Esau, and a struggle at Peniel

Jacob then sent messengers ahead to his brother Esau, to the land of Seir in the region of Edom. He instructed them, “Tell my lord Esau this: ‘Your servant Jacob sends word: I have lived as a guest with Laban and stayed on there until now. I own oxen and donkeys and flocks, and servants, men and women. I am sending to let my lord know, hoping you will look on me with favor.’” The messengers returned and told Jacob, “We reached your brother Esau. He is already coming out to meet you, with 400 men at his side.” Jacob was badly frightened and anxious. He divided his people into two camps, along with the flocks, the herds and the camels. His thought was, “If Esau falls on one camp and strikes it, the camp that is left will be able to escape.” And Jacob prayed: “God of my father Abraham, God of my father Isaac, LORD, it was you who said to me, ‘Return to your land and your family, and I will make things go well for you.’ I am far too small for all the steadfast love and faithfulness you have shown your servant. I had only a staff in my hand when I crossed this Jordan, and now I have become two camps. Rescue me from my brother, from Esau’s hand. I fear that he will come and strike us all down, mothers and children together. Yet you yourself said, ‘I will surely make things go well for you, and I will make your descendants like the sand of the sea, beyond counting for their number.’” After spending the night there, he chose from his possessions a present for his brother Esau: 200 female goats and twenty male goats, 200 ewes and twenty rams, thirty camels with their nursing young, forty cows and ten bulls, twenty female donkeys and ten male donkeys. He handed them over to his servants, one drove at a time, and told them, “Cross ahead of me, and leave a gap between each drove and the next.” To the leading servant he said, “My brother Esau will meet you and ask, ‘Whose man are you? Where are you headed? And whose animals are these you are driving?’ Then you will say, ‘Your servant Jacob’s. This is a present he is sending to my lord Esau, and Jacob himself is following us.’” He gave the same command to the second, to the third, and to everyone who walked behind the droves: “This is what you are to tell Esau when you come upon him. Add this: ‘Your servant Jacob is right behind us.’” His plan was, “I will win him over with the present that goes ahead of me, and then I will meet him face to face. It may be that he will receive me kindly.” So the gift went on ahead of him, while he stayed the night in the camp. During that night he rose, took his two wives, his two female servants and his eleven sons, and crossed at the ford of the Jabbok. He took them and sent them over the stream, along with everything he owned. Jacob stayed behind by himself. And a man wrestled with him there until dawn began to break. The man, seeing that he could not get the upper hand over Jacob, struck him at the hip socket, and Jacob’s hip was wrenched out of joint while they wrestled. “Let me go,” said the man, “for the dawn is coming up.” Jacob said, “I will not let you go unless you bless me.” The man asked him, “What is your name?” He said, “Jacob.” He said, “You will be called Jacob no longer. Your name is Israel, for you have contended with God and with people and have come through victorious.” Then Jacob asked him, “Tell me, please, what your name is.” He replied, “Why is it that you ask for my name?” And there he blessed Jacob. Jacob named the place Peniel. “I have seen God face to face,” he said, “and my life has been rescued.” The sun was rising on him as he went past Penuel, and he went limping on his injured hip. This is the reason the people of Israel still do not eat the sinew on the hip socket: Jacob’s hip socket was struck at that sinew.

fields.title: Genesis 33
fields.body_html:
Jacob meets Esau

When Jacob looked up, he saw Esau approaching with four hundred men. So he shared out the children among Leah, Rachel and the two female servants. He placed the female servants with their children at the front, Leah with hers behind them, and Rachel with Joseph at the very back. Jacob himself went ahead of them all, and on his way toward his brother he bowed to the ground seven times. But Esau ran to meet him and hugged him; he held him close and kissed him, and they wept together. Esau looked up, and when he saw the women and children he asked, “Who are all these with you?” “They are the children God has favored your servant with,” Jacob said. Then the female servants came forward with their children and bowed low. Leah and her children came forward next and bowed, and last of all Joseph and Rachel came forward and bowed. “And what were all those herds I ran into?” Esau asked. “They were meant to win my lord’s goodwill,” Jacob replied. “I have a great deal, my brother,” said Esau. “Let what is yours stay yours.” “Please, no,” Jacob said. “If you look on me with favor, take my gift from my hand. Looking on your face has been like looking on the face of God, so graciously have you received me. So take, I beg you, the blessing that was brought to you. God has been good to me, and I lack nothing.” Jacob would not take no for an answer, and Esau accepted it. Esau said, “Come, let us break camp and move on. I will go alongside you.” But Jacob said to him, “As my lord can see, the children are small, and I have to look after sheep, goats and cattle that are suckling their young. If they are pushed too hard for even a single day, the whole flock will die. Please, my lord, go on ahead of your servant. I will follow slowly, as fast as the animals in front of me and the children can go, until I reach my lord in Seir.” Esau said, “At least let me leave some of the people who are with me to go with you.” “What need is there for that?” Jacob replied. “Only let me keep my lord’s goodwill.” That day Esau turned back and took the road to Seir. Jacob for his part journeyed on to Succoth. He built a house to live in there and put up booths for his herds, and so the place got the name Succoth.

Jacob settles at Shechem

Jacob arrived safe and sound at the city of Shechem in the land of Canaan, on his return from Paddan-aram, and he set up camp just outside the city. He bought the piece of ground where he had pitched his tent from the sons of Hamor, Shechem’s father, paying a hundred pieces of silver. He erected an altar there and gave it the name El-Elohe-Israel, “God is the God of Israel”.

fields.title: Genesis 34
fields.body_html:
Dinah and the men of Shechem

One day Dinah, Jacob’s daughter by Leah, went out to get to know the young women of that country. Shechem, the son of Hamor the Hivite who ruled that region, caught sight of her. He seized her and forced her to lie with him, and so he shamed her. But then he became deeply attached to Dinah, Jacob’s daughter. He fell in love with the girl and spoke to her gently to win her heart. So Shechem went to his father Hamor and said, “Arrange for me to marry this girl.” Jacob learned that Shechem had defiled his daughter Dinah, but his sons were out in the fields with his herds, so he held his peace until they returned. Meanwhile Hamor, Shechem’s father, came out to Jacob to discuss the matter with him. Jacob’s sons came in from the fields when they heard the news. They were deeply hurt and burning with anger, for Shechem had done a vile thing in Israel in lying with Jacob’s daughter, a deed that is never to be done. Hamor talked with them and said, “My son Shechem has given his heart to your daughter. I ask you, let him marry her. Join with us in marriage. You can give your daughters to our men and take our daughters for your own. You can live among us. Settle here, move about freely, and buy property of your own; the whole land lies before you.” Then Shechem spoke up to Dinah’s father and brothers: “Be kind to me, and I will pay anything you name. Ask as high a bride-price and as rich a gift as you want, and I will pay whatever you say. Just let me have the girl for my wife.” Jacob’s sons gave Shechem and his father Hamor a deceitful answer, because Shechem had defiled their sister Dinah. They told them, “We cannot do such a thing. To give our sister to a man who is not circumcised would bring shame on us. There is only one way we will consent: you must become as we are, and every male among you must be circumcised. Then we will give you our daughters and take your daughters as wives, and we will live among you as one people. But if you refuse to be circumcised as we ask, we will take our daughter and be on our way.” Hamor and his son Shechem liked what they heard. The young man did not wait to carry out the condition, so taken was he with Jacob’s daughter. He was the most respected person in his whole family. So Hamor and his son Shechem went to the city gate and addressed the men of the town. “These people mean us no harm,” they said. “Let them live here and do business in the land; there is room enough and to spare for them. We can take their daughters as wives and give them our daughters. But there is one condition before the men will consent to live with us and become one people: every male among us has to be circumcised, just as they are. Think of it: their herds, their goods and all their animals will end up belonging to us. We have only to say yes to them, and they will make their home with us.” All the men who went in and out of the city gate agreed with Hamor and his son Shechem, and every male of the town, every one of those men, was circumcised. On the third day, while the men were still sore, two of Jacob’s sons, Simeon and Levi, Dinah’s full brothers, took up their swords. They walked into the city without any resistance and put every male to death. Hamor and his son Shechem they struck down with the sword. Then they brought Dinah out of Shechem’s house and went away. The rest of Jacob’s sons came over the bodies of the dead and looted the city, since it was there their sister had been defiled. They carried off their sheep and goats, their cattle and their donkeys, everything in the town and in the countryside. All their goods, all their little children and their wives they took as captives and loot, along with everything inside the houses. Then Jacob said to Simeon and Levi, “You have brought ruin on me. You have made me hateful to the people who live here, the Canaanites and the Perizzites. My men are few. If those peoples band together and come against me, they will wipe out me and my whole family.” But they answered, “Was he to be allowed to use our sister as if she were a prostitute?”

fields.title: Genesis 35
fields.body_html:
Jacob returns to Bethel

Then God said to Jacob, “Up, and go to Bethel, and make your home there. Build an altar there to the God who appeared to you as you fled from your brother Esau.” So Jacob told his family and everyone with him, “Get rid of every foreign god you have among you. Make yourselves clean and put on fresh clothes. Then let us set out and go up to Bethel. I will make an altar there to the God who answered me when I was in trouble and has stayed with me on every road I have traveled.” They handed over to Jacob all the foreign gods they had, along with the rings from their ears, and Jacob buried them under the great tree near Shechem. As they moved on, a dread sent by God came over the towns around them, and no one went after Jacob’s sons. Jacob arrived at Luz in the land of Canaan, the place now known as Bethel, together with all the people in his company. There he built an altar and named the place El-Bethel, “God of Bethel”, because it was there God had shown himself to him as he was fleeing from his brother. Deborah, who had nursed Rebekah, died there and was buried beneath the oak below Bethel. So the tree came to be called Allon-bacuth, “Oak of Weeping”.

Jacob named Israel, and the deaths of Rachel and Isaac

Now that Jacob had come back from Paddan-aram, God appeared to him once more and blessed him. God said to him, “Your name is Jacob, but from now on that will not be your name. Your name will be Israel.” So he gave him the name Israel. God also said to him, “I am God Almighty. Be fruitful and grow in number. A nation, a whole assembly of nations, will come from you, and kings will be born from your line. The land that I gave to Abraham and to Isaac is yours; I give it to you, and to your descendants after you I will give the land.” And God rose and left him there, at the place where he had been speaking with him. There, where God had spoken with him, Jacob raised a standing stone, and he poured a drink offering over it and oil as well. And the place where God had spoken with him, Jacob called Bethel. They moved on from Bethel, and while there was still a stretch of road left before Ephrath, Rachel’s time came, and her labor was very hard. When her labor was at its worst, the midwife told her, “Do not be afraid; this one is a son for you too.” As her life was slipping away, for she was dying, she called him Ben-oni, “son of my sorrow”. His father, though, called him Benjamin, “son of the right hand”. Rachel died and was laid to rest beside the road to Ephrath, that is, Bethlehem. Jacob raised a standing stone over her grave; it is the stone of Rachel’s grave, and it stands there to this day. Israel traveled on and pitched his tent on the far side of Migdal-eder. During Israel’s stay in that land, Reuben went and lay with Bilhah, his father’s concubine, and word of it reached Israel. There were twelve sons of Jacob. Leah’s sons were Reuben, Jacob’s firstborn, then Simeon, Levi, Judah, Issachar and Zebulun. Rachel’s sons were Joseph and Benjamin. The sons of Bilhah, Rachel’s servant, were Dan and Naphtali. The sons of Zilpah, Leah’s servant, were Gad and Asher. These were Jacob’s sons, born to him in Paddan-aram. Jacob finally reached his father Isaac at Mamre, by Kiriath-arba (that is, Hebron), where first Abraham and then Isaac had lived as foreigners. Isaac lived to the age of 180. Isaac’s breath failed, and he died and was gathered to his people, an old man who had his fill of years. His sons Esau and Jacob laid him in the grave.

fields.title: Genesis 36
fields.body_html:
The family of Esau

This is the account of the family of Esau, that is, Edom. Esau married women of Canaan: Adah daughter of Elon the Hittite, Oholibamah daughter of Anah and granddaughter of Zibeon the Hivite, and Basemath daughter of Ishmael, Nebaioth’s sister. Adah bore Esau a son, Eliphaz, and Basemath bore Reuel. Oholibamah bore Jeush, Jalam and Korah. These were Esau’s sons, born to him in the land of Canaan. Esau took his wives, his sons and daughters, everyone in his household, his herds and all his animals, and all the goods he had gained in Canaan, and went away to another land, apart from his brother Jacob. They had too much wealth to live side by side; the land where they were living as foreigners could not feed all their herds. So Esau settled in the hill country of Seir. Esau is Edom. This is the account of the family of Esau, ancestor of the Edomites, in the hill country of Seir. These are the names of Esau’s sons: Eliphaz, son of Esau’s wife Adah, and Reuel, son of Esau’s wife Basemath. The sons of Eliphaz were Teman, Omar, Zepho, Gatam and Kenaz. Timna, a concubine of Esau’s son Eliphaz, bore him Amalek. These were the descendants of Esau’s wife Adah. The sons of Reuel were Nahath, Zerah, Shammah and Mizzah. These were the descendants of Esau’s wife Basemath. The sons of Esau’s wife Oholibamah, daughter of Anah and granddaughter of Zibeon, were Jeush, Jalam and Korah, whom she bore to Esau. These were the clan chiefs among Esau’s descendants. From the sons of Eliphaz, Esau’s firstborn, came the chiefs Teman, Omar, Zepho, Kenaz, Korah, Gatam and Amalek. These were the chiefs descended from Eliphaz in the land of Edom, the descendants of Adah. From the sons of Reuel, Esau’s son, came the chiefs Nahath, Zerah, Shammah and Mizzah. These were the chiefs descended from Reuel in the land of Edom, the descendants of Esau’s wife Basemath. From the sons of Esau’s wife Oholibamah came the chiefs Jeush, Jalam and Korah. These were the chiefs descended from Esau’s wife Oholibamah, Anah’s daughter. These are the sons of Esau, that is, Edom, and these are their chiefs.

The sons of Seir the Horite

These were the sons of Seir the Horite, the people who already lived in the land: Lotan, Shobal, Zibeon, Anah, Dishon, Ezer and Dishan. These were the Horite chiefs, the sons of Seir in the land of Edom. The sons of Lotan were Hori and Hemam, and Lotan’s sister was Timna. The sons of Shobal were Alvan, Manahath, Ebal, Shepho and Onam. The sons of Zibeon were Aiah and Anah. This was the Anah who discovered the hot springs in the wilderness while he was grazing his father Zibeon’s donkeys. The children of Anah were Dishon and Oholibamah, Anah’s daughter. The sons of Dishon were Hemdan, Eshban, Ithran and Cheran. The sons of Ezer were Bilhan, Zaavan and Akan. The sons of Dishan were Uz and Aran. These were the Horite chiefs: Lotan, Shobal, Zibeon, Anah, Dishon, Ezer and Dishan. These were the Horite chiefs, clan by clan, in the land of Seir.

The kings of Edom

These are the kings who ruled in Edom before any king ruled over the people of Israel: Bela son of Beor was king in Edom; his city was named Dinhabah. When Bela died, Jobab son of Zerah, from Bozrah, became king in his place. When Jobab died, Husham from the land of the Temanites became king in his place. When Husham died, Hadad son of Bedad, who beat the Midianites in battle in the land of Moab, became king in his place. His city was named Avith. When Hadad died, Samlah from Masrekah became king in his place. When Samlah died, Shaul from Rehoboth on the River became king in his place. When Shaul died, Baal-hanan son of Achbor became king in his place. When Baal-hanan son of Achbor died, Hadar became king in his place. His city was named Pau, and his wife was Mehetabel, the daughter of Matred and granddaughter of Mezahab. These are the names of the chiefs descended from Esau, listed by clan and region, each by name: Timna, Alvah, Jetheth, Oholibamah, Elah, Pinon, Kenaz, Teman, Mibzar, Magdiel and Iram. These were the chiefs of Edom, by their settlements in the land they held. This was Esau, ancestor of the Edomites.

fields.title: Genesis 37
fields.body_html:
Joseph and his brothers

Jacob stayed on in the land where his father had lived as a foreigner, the land of Canaan. This is the story of Jacob’s family. When Joseph was seventeen, he used to tend the flocks with his brothers, working as a helper alongside the sons of Bilhah and Zilpah, two of his father’s wives. Joseph brought their father an unfavorable report about them. Israel loved Joseph more than any of his other sons, since he had been born to him in his old age, and he had a long-sleeved robe made for him. His brothers saw that their father loved him more than any of them, and they hated him so much that they could not say a friendly word to him. Then Joseph had a dream, and when he told it to his brothers, their hatred of him grew worse. “Listen to this dream I had,” he said to them. “We were out in the field tying up bundles of grain, when all at once my bundle got up and stood on end, and your bundles came around it and bowed low before it.” His brothers answered, “So you think you will be king over us, do you? Are you going to be our master?” And they hated him all the more because of his dreams and the way he told them. Then he had a second dream and told that one to his brothers as well. “Listen,” he said, “I have had another dream. This time the sun and the moon and eleven stars were bowing to me.” When he told it to his father as well as his brothers, his father scolded him. “What sort of dream is this?” he said. “Are your mother and I and your brothers really going to come and bow to the ground in front of you?” His brothers envied him, but his father did not forget what he had said. One time his brothers had gone to graze their father’s flocks near Shechem. Israel said to Joseph, “Your brothers are grazing the flocks near Shechem, are they not? Come, I am going to send you to them.” “I am ready,” Joseph replied. “Go and find out how your brothers are doing and how the flocks are,” he said, “and come back and tell me.” So he sent him off from the valley of Hebron, and Joseph made his way to Shechem. A man came upon him wandering around in the countryside and asked him, “What are you looking for?” “It is my brothers I am trying to find,” he answered. “Can you tell me where they are grazing their flocks?” “They have left here,” the man said. “I heard them say, ‘Let us go on to Dothan.’” So Joseph followed his brothers and caught up with them at Dothan. They spotted him while he was still far off, and before he reached them they schemed to put him to death. “Here comes the great dreamer,” they said to one another. “Come on, let us kill him now and toss him into one of these cisterns. We can say a wild beast ate him. Then we will find out what comes of his dreams!” When Reuben heard this, he tried to save Joseph from them. “We must not kill him,” he said. “Do not shed his blood,” Reuben told them. “Throw him into this cistern out here in the wild, but do not lay a hand on him.” He meant to rescue him from them and take him back to his father. So when Joseph reached his brothers, they tore off his robe, the long-sleeved robe he was wearing, and they grabbed him and threw him into the cistern. The cistern was empty; it had no water in it. Then they sat down to their meal. Looking up, they saw a caravan of Ishmaelites coming from Gilead, their camels loaded with gum, balm and resin, which they were taking down to Egypt. Judah said to his brothers, “What do we gain by killing our brother and hiding the blood? Let us sell him to the Ishmaelites instead and keep our own hands off him. After all, he is our brother, our own flesh and blood.” His brothers agreed. When the Midianite traders came by, they pulled Joseph up out of the cistern and sold him to the Ishmaelites for about 8 ounces of silver, and they took Joseph away to Egypt. When Reuben came back to the cistern and saw that Joseph was gone, he tore his clothes in grief. He went back to his brothers and said, “The boy is gone! And I, what am I going to do?” They took Joseph’s robe, killed a young goat, and soaked the robe in its blood. They sent the long-sleeved robe to their father with the message, “We found this. Look it over and see whether it is your son’s robe or not.” He knew it at once. “It is my son’s robe!” he cried. “Some wild animal has eaten him. Joseph has been torn apart, there is no doubt of it!” Jacob tore his clothes, wrapped sackcloth around his waist, and grieved for his son a long time. All his sons and daughters came to comfort him, but he would not be consoled. “No,” he said, “I will go down to the grave still mourning for my son.” And so his father wept for him. Meanwhile the Midianites had sold Joseph in Egypt to Potiphar, one of Pharaoh’s officials, the commander of his guard.

fields.title: Genesis 38
fields.body_html:
Judah and Tamar

It was at about this time that Judah parted company with his brothers. He went down and pitched his tent near Hirah, a man from the town of Adullam. There Judah caught sight of a woman, the daughter of a Canaanite called Shua. He took her as his wife and lay with her. She conceived and bore a son, and Judah called him Er. She conceived again and bore another son, whom she called Onan. Then she had yet another son, and she named him Shelah. Judah was at Kezib when she gave birth to him. For Er, his firstborn, Judah found a wife whose name was Tamar. But Judah’s firstborn, Er, was evil in the LORD’s eyes, and the LORD brought his life to an end. Judah told Onan, “Go to your brother’s widow and carry out the brother-in-law’s duty: marry her and so give your brother descendants.” Onan, however, knew that any children would not be counted as his. So each time he lay with his brother’s widow, he made sure his seed was wasted on the ground, to avoid giving his brother descendants. Onan’s deed was evil in the LORD’s eyes, and Onan too died by the LORD’s hand. Judah then said to Tamar his daughter-in-law, “Go on as a widow in your father’s house until my son Shelah is grown.” For he was thinking, “Otherwise he too may die, as his brothers did.” So Tamar went and made her home in her father’s house. Years went by, and Shua’s daughter, Judah’s wife, died. After he had been consoled, Judah went up to Timnah with his friend Hirah from Adullam, to be with the men shearing his flocks. Word reached Tamar: “Your father-in-law is going up to Timnah for the shearing of his sheep.” So she laid aside her widow’s clothing, put on a veil and wrapped herself up, and took a seat at the gateway of Enaim, which lies on the road to Timnah. She could see that Shelah was now grown, and still she had not been given to him as his wife. Judah saw her and took her for a prostitute, since her face was veiled. He turned off the road toward her. “Come,” he said, “let me lie with you.” He did not know she was his daughter-in-law. “And what will you give me for it?” she answered. “I will have a young goat sent to you from the flock,” he said.
