She answered, “Yes, if you hand me something to keep as a guarantee until you send it.” “What do you want as security?” he asked. “Your seal on its cord,” she said, “and the staff in your hand.” So he handed them over and lay with her, and she conceived a child by him. Then she rose and went away. She laid aside her veil and put her widow’s clothing back on. Judah had his friend the Adullamite take the young goat, so as to get back the pledge from the woman, but the friend found no trace of her. He inquired of the local men, “The shrine prostitute who sat by the roadside at Enaim, where is she?” They replied, “We have had no shrine prostitute here.” He came back to Judah and reported, “I did not find her. What is more, the local men said, ‘We have had no shrine prostitute here.’” “Let her have the things, then,” said Judah. “We do not want people laughing at us. As you know, I sent this young goat, and you could not find her.” Some three months went by. Then word came to Judah: “Tamar, your daughter-in-law, has prostituted herself, and she is even pregnant from it.” “Take her out,” Judah ordered, “and let her be burned.” Even as she was being led out, she sent this word to her father-in-law: “The man these things belong to is the one who made me pregnant.” She added, “Please examine them. Whose are they, this seal and cord and staff?” Judah saw that they were his. “She has been more righteous than I have,” he said, “because I would not let her marry my son Shelah.” He never had relations with her again. When her time of delivery came, there were twins in her womb. During the birth one baby reached out a hand. The midwife caught hold of it and bound a scarlet thread on it, saying, “This is the first one out.” Then the hand was drawn back, and his brother came out instead. “What a breakthrough you have forced for yourself!” said the midwife. And so he was named Perez. Next his brother was born, the scarlet thread still on his hand, and he received the name Zerah.

fields.title: Genesis 39
fields.body_html:
Joseph and Potiphar’s wife

Meanwhile Joseph had been carried down to Egypt. The Ishmaelites who brought him there sold him to Potiphar, an Egyptian who served Pharaoh as a court officer and commanded his guard. The LORD was with Joseph, and he became a successful man while he served in the house of the Egyptian, his master. His master noticed that the LORD was with him, and that whatever Joseph undertook, the LORD made it turn out well. Joseph won his master’s approval and waited on him personally. Then his master made him overseer of his household and handed over to him everything he possessed. As soon as Joseph had charge of the house and of all the Egyptian owned, the LORD blessed that household on Joseph’s account. Whatever the man had, at home or in the fields, the LORD’s blessing rested on it. So the Egyptian left everything he owned in Joseph’s hands. Having Joseph, he gave no thought to anything but the food he ate. Joseph had a fine figure and a handsome face. Some time later his master’s wife set her eyes on Joseph. “Sleep with me,” she said. He refused. “You see,” he said to his master’s wife, “with me here, my master gives no thought to what goes on in the house. He has put everything he owns under my care. He does not rank above me in this house. The only thing he has denied me is you, since you are his wife. How could I commit so great a wrong, and sin against God?” She urged Joseph day after day, but he would not listen to her or agree to lie beside her or be in her company. But one day, as Joseph came into the house to see to his work, with none of the men of the household there inside, she seized hold of his garment. “Sleep with me!” she said. But he ran from her and got outside, leaving the garment in her grip. When she saw that he had run outside and left his garment in her hand, she summoned the men of her household and said to them, “See here! He has brought in a Hebrew to toy with us. The man came in to me to lie with me, and I screamed at the top of my voice. Hearing me raise my voice and shout, he left his garment beside me and fled outside.” She put the garment down beside her and waited for Joseph’s master to come home. Then she repeated it all to him: “The Hebrew slave whom you brought among us came in to me, to make a plaything of me. But as I raised my voice and cried out, he abandoned his garment beside me and fled outside.” Joseph’s master listened to his wife telling him, “That is what your slave did to me,” and he flew into a rage. He had Joseph taken and locked up in the prison house used for the king’s prisoners, and there Joseph remained. But the LORD was with Joseph. He treated him with loyal kindness and won him the favor of the prison warden. The warden handed over to Joseph the care of every prisoner in the place, and Joseph directed all the work that was done there. The warden never looked into anything entrusted to Joseph, for the LORD was with him, and whatever Joseph did, the LORD made it succeed.

fields.title: Genesis 40
fields.body_html:
The cupbearer’s and the baker’s dreams

After this, two men in the service of the king of Egypt, his cupbearer and his baker, did wrong against their master. Pharaoh’s anger was roused against these two officials of his, the chief cupbearer and the chief baker. He placed them under guard at the house of the commander of the guard, in the very prison where Joseph was being held. The commander of the guard assigned Joseph to them, and he waited on them. They remained in custody for some time. Then, on the same night, both prisoners dreamed, the king of Egypt’s cupbearer and his baker. Each had his own dream, and each dream called for its own interpretation. Joseph came in to them the next morning and could see how troubled they looked. He questioned the two officials of Pharaoh who were confined with him in his master’s house: “Why are your faces so gloomy today?” “Each of us has had a dream,” they replied, “and we have no one to interpret them.” Joseph said, “Is it not God who gives interpretations? Please, tell me about them.” So the chief cupbearer told his dream to Joseph, saying, “There I was, dreaming, and before me stood a vine, with three branches on it. No sooner had it sprouted than it was in bloom, and its clusters were soon full of ripe grapes. In my hand I had Pharaoh’s cup. I gathered the grapes, pressed them out into the cup, and set it in Pharaoh’s hand.” Joseph said to him, “Here is the interpretation: the three branches stand for three days. Three days from now Pharaoh will lift up your head and reinstate you, and you will hand Pharaoh his cup as in the old days, when you served as his cupbearer. And once things go well for you, keep me in mind. Please do me this kindness: speak of me to Pharaoh and have me brought out of this place. The truth is that I was kidnapped from the land of the Hebrews. And here, too, I have done nothing wrong that should have landed me in this pit.” The chief baker, seeing that the interpretation was a good one, said to Joseph, “I also had a dream. I was carrying three baskets of white bread on my head. The top basket held every sort of baked food for Pharaoh, and the birds kept pecking at it from the basket on my head.” Joseph replied, “Here is the interpretation: the three baskets stand for three days. Three days from now Pharaoh will lift up your head, right off your body, and hang you on a pole, and the birds will eat the flesh from your bones.” The third day came, and it was Pharaoh’s birthday. He held a banquet for all his officials, and with them all present he lifted up the head of the chief cupbearer and the head of the chief baker. He reinstated the chief cupbearer in his office, and the cupbearer went back to placing the cup in Pharaoh’s hand. The chief baker, though, he hanged, exactly as Joseph had explained to them. But the chief cupbearer gave no thought to Joseph; he put him out of his mind.

fields.title: Genesis 41
fields.body_html:
Pharaoh’s dreams, and Joseph put in charge of Egypt

Two whole years later Pharaoh had a dream. He was standing beside the Nile, and seven cows came climbing up out of the river, handsome and plump, and began feeding in the marsh grass. Then seven other cows came up from the Nile behind them, poor-looking and scrawny, and stood next to the first cows on the riverbank. And the ugly, scrawny cows devoured the seven handsome, plump ones. At that Pharaoh awoke. Once he was asleep again, he dreamed a second time: seven ears of grain, plump and fine, were growing up on one stalk. Then seven other ears came up behind them, thin and burnt dry by the east wind. And the thin ears gulped down the seven plump, full ones. Then Pharaoh woke up and found that he had been dreaming. When morning came, Pharaoh was uneasy in spirit. He summoned every magician and wise man in Egypt and described his dream to them, but none of them could tell Pharaoh what it meant. Then the chief cupbearer spoke up and said to Pharaoh, “Today I must bring up my own faults. There was a time when Pharaoh was angry with his officials, the chief baker and me, and he had us held in custody in the house of the commander of the guard. On the same night he and I each had a dream, and each dream carried a meaning that fit the man who dreamed it. With us in custody was a young Hebrew, a slave of the commander of the guard. We described our dreams to him, and he explained them, telling each man what his own dream meant. Everything happened just as he said it would: Pharaoh put me back in my post, and he hanged the baker.” So Pharaoh summoned Joseph, and they hurried him up out of the prison pit. Joseph shaved, put on clean clothes, and went in to Pharaoh. Pharaoh said to Joseph, “I have had a dream, and nobody can tell me what it means. Word has reached me that you only need to hear a dream to explain it.” Joseph answered Pharaoh, “It is not in my power. God will give Pharaoh an answer for his good.” So Pharaoh began to describe it to Joseph: “There I was in my dream, standing at the edge of the Nile. Up out of the river came seven cows, plump and handsome, and they fed in the marsh grass. Seven more cows came up behind them, weak, very ugly and all skin and bone. In all the land of Egypt I have never seen cows so bad. And the lean and ugly cows devoured the first seven, the fat ones. Yet once the fat cows were inside them, nobody would have known it; they looked as wretched as they had at first. Then I awoke. Then, in my dream, I saw a single stalk with seven ears of grain on it, full and fine. Behind them sprang up seven more ears, shriveled, thin and burnt dry by the east wind. And the thin ears gulped down the seven good ones. I described all this to the magicians, and not one of them could tell me what it meant.” Then Joseph said to Pharaoh, “Pharaoh’s dreams carry a single message. God has told Pharaoh ahead of time what he is going to do. The seven good cows stand for seven years, and so do the seven good ears of grain. It is all one dream. Likewise the seven scrawny, ugly cows that followed them mean seven years, and the seven empty ears dried out by the east wind mean seven years of famine. That is what I told Pharaoh: God has let Pharaoh see in advance what he is about to do. Seven years are coming in which all Egypt will have a great abundance. But after them will come seven years of famine. People will forget there was ever plenty in Egypt, and the famine will exhaust the land. The plenty will not even be noticed in the land, so crushing will the famine be that comes after it. Pharaoh dreamed it twice because God has fixed this in place, and God will waste no time in carrying it out. So Pharaoh should now choose someone with understanding and wisdom, and give him authority over the land of Egypt. Pharaoh should act now to place supervisors over the land and collect a fifth of Egypt’s harvest during the seven good years. Let them collect every bit of food from the good years now coming, and stockpile grain in the cities under Pharaoh’s control, guarding it as a food supply. This food will then be a stockpile for the land to draw on during the seven years of famine that Egypt will face, and the land will not be wiped out by the famine.” This advice pleased Pharaoh and all his officials. Pharaoh asked his officials, “Could we ever find another man like this one, a man who has the spirit of God in him?” Then Pharaoh turned to Joseph. “God has let you know all of this,” he said, “so there is nobody with your insight and wisdom. You will run my household, and all my people will do as you say. The throne alone will set me above you.” And Pharaoh told Joseph, “Look, I am placing you over all the land of Egypt.” Pharaoh slipped the signet ring off his hand and placed it on Joseph’s. He had him dressed in clothes of fine linen and hung a gold chain on his neck. He let him ride in the chariot that was second only to his own, and men called out ahead of him, “Bow down!” In this way Pharaoh set him over the entire land of Egypt. “I am Pharaoh,” he told Joseph, “and yet no one anywhere in Egypt will so much as move a hand or a foot unless you allow it.” Pharaoh renamed Joseph Zaphenath-paneah and married him to Asenath, the daughter of Potiphera, priest of On. And Joseph went out to take charge of the land of Egypt. Joseph was thirty years old when he took up his post before Pharaoh, king of Egypt. Leaving the king’s presence, Joseph made a tour of the whole land of Egypt. In the seven years of plenty the land produced heaping handfuls. Throughout those seven years in Egypt Joseph gathered up all the food and laid it up in the cities. Every city received the food from its own surrounding fields. Joseph amassed grain in huge quantities, as plentiful as the sand by the sea. In the end he gave up counting it, for there was too much to count. Two sons were born to Joseph before the first year of famine came. Their mother was Asenath, daughter of Potiphera, priest of On. Joseph called his firstborn son Manasseh, “because,” he said, “God has let me forget all my hardship and my father’s whole household.” The second son he called Ephraim, “because,” he said, “God has made me fruitful in the country where I was afflicted.” The seven years of plenty that Egypt had enjoyed came to an end. Then the seven years of famine set in, as Joseph had said they would. Famine struck every land around, yet all over Egypt people still had food. Before long the whole land of Egypt felt the hunger too, and the people appealed to Pharaoh for food. Pharaoh’s answer to all Egypt was, “Go to Joseph. Whatever he tells you, do it.” The famine covered the whole face of the land. Joseph threw open every place where grain was stored and began selling it to the Egyptians, and the famine kept its hard grip on Egypt. The whole world came to Joseph in Egypt to buy grain, since the famine had tightened its hold everywhere on earth.

fields.title: Genesis 42
fields.body_html:
Joseph’s brothers go down to Egypt

Jacob saw that grain was to be had in Egypt, and he asked his sons, “Why do you keep staring at one another?” He said, “I am told there is grain in Egypt. Go down there and buy us grain, so that we stay alive and do not die.” Ten of Joseph’s brothers set off down to Egypt for grain. But Jacob kept Benjamin, Joseph’s brother, at home and did not send him with the others, because he was afraid something might happen to him. The sons of Israel came to buy grain along with everyone else who was coming, because the famine had reached the land of Canaan. Joseph was the man in power over the country, and he oversaw the sale of grain to all its people. Joseph’s brothers came in and bowed low before him, their faces to the ground. Joseph knew his brothers the moment he saw them, but he treated them like strangers and spoke to them sternly. He demanded, “Where have you come from?” They said, “We have come from Canaan to buy food.” Joseph knew his brothers, but they had no idea who he was. Joseph called to mind the dreams he had dreamed about them. “You are spies,” he told them. “You came to look for the weak spots in our country’s defenses.” “Not at all, my lord,” they protested. “Your servants have come for nothing but food. We are all brothers, sons of one father, and we are honest men. Your servants are no spies.” “Not so,” he told them. “You have come to spy out where the land is unguarded.” They answered, “There are twelve of us, your servants, all brothers, sons of one man in the land of Canaan. The youngest is at home with our father just now, and one brother is gone.” “It is exactly what I said,” Joseph told them. “You are spies. Here is how I will test you. I swear by Pharaoh’s life that you will not get out of here until your youngest brother shows up. Pick one of you to go and bring your brother back, and the others will be held in prison. Then we will find out whether there is any truth in what you say. If there is not, I swear by Pharaoh’s life, you are spies!” Then he locked them all up together for three days. On the third day Joseph told them, “I am a God-fearing man, so if you do what I say, you will live. If you are as honest as you say, let one of your brothers stay locked up where you have been held, and the others may go and carry grain home to feed your hungry families. Then bring your youngest brother to me. That way what you have said will be proved true, and you will not have to die.” And they agreed to this. They said to each other, “We really are guilty over what we did to our brother. We watched his anguish as he begged us for mercy, and we refused to listen. Now this same anguish has come down on us.” Reuben broke in, “I told you, did I not, not to harm the boy? You would not hear of it. And now his blood is being demanded back from us.” They had no idea that Joseph understood them, since he had been speaking to them through an interpreter. Joseph stepped away from them and wept. When he came back, he talked with them again, then picked out Simeon and had him tied up right in front of them. Joseph ordered his men to fill the brothers’ containers with grain, to slip each man’s money back into his sack, and to give them food for the road. They did all this for them. They loaded the grain onto their donkeys and set off. When they stopped for the night, one of them opened his sack to feed his donkey and saw his money lying at the top of the sack. He called to his brothers, “Someone has given my money back! Look, it is right here in my sack!” Their courage failed them. They turned to one another, shaking, and asked, “What has God done to us?” Back home with their father Jacob in the land of Canaan, they gave him a full account of all that had happened to them. “The man who rules that country was harsh with us. He accused us of coming to spy out the land. We told him, ‘We are honest. We are no spies. There were twelve of us brothers, all sons of one father. One is gone, and the youngest is at home with our father in Canaan right now.’ Then the man, the ruler of the land, told us, ‘This is how I will know you are honest. One of your brothers stays here with me; the rest of you take what your hungry families need and go. And bring me your youngest brother; then I will be sure you are honest men and no spies. I will hand your brother back to you, and you may move about the country and do business.’” Then they began emptying their sacks, and in each man’s sack lay his purse of money. When they and their father saw the purses, fear came over them. Their father Jacob said to them, “You are leaving me childless! Joseph is no more, Simeon is no more, and now you would take Benjamin from me too. All of it lands on me!” Reuben told his father, “If I do not bring him home to you, you can kill my own two sons. Leave him in my charge, and I will see that he comes back to you.” But Jacob said, “My son will not go down with you. His brother is dead, and he alone remains. If anything happened to him on your journey, you would bring me, gray-haired, down to the grave in grief.”

fields.title: Genesis 43
fields.body_html:
The second journey, with Benjamin

Meanwhile the famine lay heavy on the land. Once the grain they had brought back from Egypt was all eaten, their father told them, “Go back again and get us a little food.” Judah answered him, “The man warned us in the strongest terms, ‘Do not show yourselves before me unless your brother comes with you.’ Let our brother come with us, and we will go down and get food for you. But if you refuse to send him, we will not go, for the man’s words to us were, ‘Unless your brother is with you, you will not see my face.’” Israel said, “Why did you do me such harm? Why did you have to tell the man there was another brother?” They said, “The man pressed us with questions about ourselves and our relatives: ‘Is your father still alive? Have you a brother?’ All we did was answer what he asked. How could we have guessed he would tell us, ‘Bring your brother down’?” Judah said to his father Israel, “Send the boy with me, and let us set out now. Then we will stay alive and not die, all of us: we, you and our little ones. I pledge myself for him. Demand him back from me. If I fail to bring him home and stand him before your eyes, the guilt will be mine before you as long as I live. If we had not wasted all this time, we could have been there and back twice by now.” Their father Israel told them, “Since there is no other way, here is what you must do. Pack some of the choicest things our land produces and take them down to the man as a gift: a little balm and a little honey, gum and resin, pistachios and almonds. Carry twice the money with you, and give back the money you found at the top of your sacks; it may have been an oversight. Take your brother as well. Get up and return to the man. May God Almighty stir the man’s heart to mercy toward you, so that he releases your other brother to you, and Benjamin too. As for me, if I must lose my children, then I lose them.” The men took the gift, took twice the money, and took Benjamin. Then they set off down to Egypt and stood before Joseph. As soon as Joseph saw Benjamin among them, he told the man in charge of his household, “Bring these men into the house. Have an animal butchered and a meal made ready; they will be dining with me at noon.” The steward carried out Joseph’s orders and led the brothers into Joseph’s house. Being taken into Joseph’s house terrified the men. They said to themselves, “This is about the money that turned up in our sacks last time. He has brought us in here to turn on us and fall on us, make us his slaves, and take our donkeys.” At the doorway of the house they came up to the man in charge of Joseph’s household and spoke to him. “Excuse us, my lord,” they said. “We really did come down here before, just to buy food. When we reached our night’s lodging and opened our sacks, there was each man’s money at the top of his sack, the full weight of it. Here it is; we have brought it back. We have brought other money besides, to pay for food this time. Who put our money back in our sacks, we cannot tell.” “All is well,” he replied. “Put away your fear. It was your God, the God of your father, who hid treasure in your sacks for you. Your money reached me.” And he led Simeon out to join them. The steward led them inside Joseph’s house. He brought water so they could wash their feet, and he gave their donkeys feed. Then they set out their gift, ready for when Joseph would come at noon, because they had been told they would be eating a meal there. Joseph came home, and they carried the gift they had with them into the house and presented it to him, bowing low to the ground. Joseph asked after their health. “And your father, the old man you spoke of,” he said, “is he well? Is he still alive?” “Your servant our father is in good health,” they answered. “He is still alive.” And they bowed their heads and knelt low. Then Joseph raised his eyes and caught sight of Benjamin, his brother, born of his own mother. “Is this the youngest brother you spoke to me about?” he asked. And he said, “May God show you favor, my son.” Joseph had to leave quickly; his heart was so stirred for his brother that he was close to tears. He went into an inner room, and there he wept. Then he washed his face and came out again. Holding his feelings in check, he gave the order: “Bring in the food.” Food was set out for Joseph by himself, for the brothers by themselves, and for the Egyptians who dined with him by themselves. Egyptians would not share a meal with Hebrews, since they found that abhorrent. They were seated facing him, the eldest in the place his birthright gave him and the youngest in the place that fit his youth, and the men stared at one another in amazement. Dishes were sent to them from the food in front of Joseph, and Benjamin got five times as much as any of the others. They drank with him until they were merry.

fields.title: Genesis 44
fields.body_html:
The silver cup

Joseph gave orders to the man in charge of his household: “Load these men’s sacks with all the food they are able to carry, and put every man’s money back at the top of his sack. And put my cup, the silver one, in the top of the youngest one’s sack, along with the money he paid for his grain.” The steward carried out Joseph’s instructions. At first light the men were sent off with their donkeys. They had left the city and were still close by when Joseph told his steward, “Go after those men at once. When you catch up with them, ask them, ‘Why have you paid back good with evil? Is this not the cup my master drinks from, the one he uses to read omens? What you have done is wicked.’” When he caught up with them, he repeated those words to them. “Why would my lord say such things?” they answered. “Your servants would never do anything of the kind! Remember, we brought back to you from Canaan the money we found in the tops of our sacks. Why would we then steal silver or gold from your master’s house? If any one of us is found to have it, he must die, and the rest of us will become your slaves, my lord.” “Very well,” he replied, “it will be as you have said. But only the one who has the cup will become my slave; the rest of you will go free of blame.” Each of them quickly lowered his sack to the ground and opened it. The steward searched, starting with the eldest and ending with the youngest, and the cup turned up in Benjamin’s sack. At this they tore their clothes. Then each of them loaded his donkey again, and they went back to the city. Judah and his brothers came to Joseph’s house while he was still there, and they threw themselves down on the ground before him. “What have you done?” Joseph demanded. “Did you not realize that a man in my position can find things out by divination?” “My lord, what can we say?” Judah answered. “What words do we have? How could we prove we are innocent? God has exposed your servants’ guilt. We are your slaves now, my lord, all of us, not just the one who had the cup.” But Joseph answered, “I would never do such a thing! Only the one who had the cup will be my slave. The rest of you may return safely to your father.”

Judah pleads for Benjamin

Then Judah stepped up to him and said, “Forgive me, my lord, but let your servant say something to you in private, and please do not be angry with your servant, for you are as great as Pharaoh. My lord asked your servants whether we had a father or another brother. We answered, ‘We have an elderly father, and there is a young son born to him in his old age. The boy’s brother is dead; he is the only one of his mother’s sons still living, and his father loves him dearly.’ Then you told your servants, ‘Bring him down here so I can see him for myself.’ We told my lord, ‘The boy cannot leave his father. If he did, his father would die.’ But you told your servants, ‘If your youngest brother does not come down with you, you will not be allowed to see me again.’ When we returned to your servant, my father, we reported to him everything my lord had said. Later our father told us, ‘Go back and buy us a little more food.’ But we said, ‘We cannot go down there. We will go only if our youngest brother goes with us. Unless he is with us, the man will not see us.’ Your servant my father replied, ‘You know that my wife gave me two sons. One of them left me, and I said, “He must have been torn apart by a wild animal.” And I have never seen him again. If you take this one from me too, and something happens to him, you will send this gray head of mine down to the grave in misery.’ So now, if I go back to your servant my father without the boy, since his life and the boy’s life are tied together, as soon as he sees that the boy is not with us, he will die. Your servants will have sent our father, your servant, to the grave, gray-haired and grieving. Your servant guaranteed the boy’s safety to my father. I told him, ‘If I do not bring him back to you, I will be guilty before you, Father, all my life.’ Now then, please let me, your servant, stay here as my lord’s slave instead of the boy, and let the boy go home with his brothers. How could I go back to my father without the boy? I cannot bear to watch the misery it would bring him.”

fields.title: Genesis 45
fields.body_html:
Joseph tells his brothers who he is

Joseph could hold back no longer in front of all the attendants around him. “Send everyone out of here!” he cried. So he was alone with his brothers when he told them who he was. He wept so loudly that the Egyptians heard it, and word of it reached Pharaoh’s household. “I am Joseph!” he said to his brothers. “Is my father really still alive?” His brothers were too shaken to say a word, dismayed to be standing before him. Then Joseph said to his brothers, “Please, come closer.” When they had come closer, he said, “I am your brother Joseph, the one you sold into Egypt. But now, do not be upset, and do not be angry with yourselves for selling me here. It was God who sent me on ahead of you, to keep people alive. The famine has now gripped the land for two years, and for five more years there will be no plowing and no harvest. God sent me ahead of you to make sure your family would survive on the earth, and to save your lives in a great act of rescue. So it was not really you who sent me here, but God. And he has made me a father to Pharaoh, master of his whole household and ruler of all Egypt. Go up to my father quickly and tell him, ‘This is what your son Joseph says: God has made me master of all Egypt. Come down to me without wasting any time. You can settle in the region of Goshen and be close to me, you and your children and grandchildren, your sheep and goats and cattle, and everything that belongs to you. I will supply your needs there, since there are still five years of famine ahead. Otherwise you, your family and all you have will end up in want.’ You can see for yourselves, and so can my brother Benjamin, that it is really I who am speaking to you. Tell my father about all the honor I have in Egypt and everything you have seen. And hurry, bring my father down here.” Then he threw his arms around his brother Benjamin and wept, and Benjamin wept as he embraced him. He kissed each of his brothers and wept as he held them. Only then were his brothers able to talk with him. News reached Pharaoh’s palace that Joseph’s brothers had arrived, and Pharaoh and his officials were glad. Pharaoh said to Joseph, “Tell your brothers to load up their animals and return to the land of Canaan. They are to bring their father and their families and come to me. I will give them the best land in Egypt, and they will live off the richest produce in the country. And you are to give them this order as well: take carts from Egypt for their children and their wives, and bring their father here. They need not worry about the things they leave behind, because the best of all Egypt will be theirs.” The sons of Israel did as they were told. Joseph gave them carts at Pharaoh’s command, and supplies for the road. He gave each of them a new set of clothes, but to Benjamin he gave about 7.5 pounds of silver and five sets of clothes. To his father he sent the same, and more: ten donkeys laden with the finest goods of Egypt, and ten female donkeys carrying grain, bread and food for his father’s journey. Then he sent his brothers off, and as they left he told them, “Do not argue with each other on the way.” So they left Egypt and went up to their father Jacob in the land of Canaan. “Joseph is alive!” they told him. “He is governor of the whole land of Egypt!” Jacob was stunned; he could not believe them. But when they repeated to him everything Joseph had said to them, and when he saw the carts Joseph had sent to carry him, their father Jacob’s spirit came back to life. “Enough!” said Israel. “My son Joseph is still alive! I will go and see him before I die.”

fields.title: Genesis 46
fields.body_html:
Jacob goes down to Egypt

So Israel set out, taking everything he owned. At Beersheba he stopped and offered sacrifices to the God of his father Isaac. In the night God spoke to Israel in visions. “Jacob, Jacob,” he called, and Jacob said, “Here I am.” He said, “I am God, your father’s God. Do not fear the journey down to Egypt, for it is there that I will make you a great nation. I myself will go down with you to Egypt, and I myself will bring you up again without fail. Joseph will be the one to close your eyes.” Jacob moved on from Beersheba, and the sons of Israel carried their father Jacob, their little ones and their wives in the carts that Pharaoh had sent for him. They also took the livestock and goods they had gained in the land of Canaan, and they came to Egypt, Jacob and all his descendants with him, his sons and grandsons, his daughters and granddaughters. He brought all his descendants with him to Egypt.

The family of Israel who came to Egypt

These are the names of the family of Israel who came to Egypt, Jacob and his sons. Jacob’s firstborn was Reuben. Reuben’s sons were Hanoch, Pallu, Hezron and Carmi. Simeon’s sons were Jemuel, Jamin, Ohad, Jachin and Zohar, and Shaul, whose mother was a Canaanite. Levi’s sons were Gershon, Kohath and Merari. Judah’s sons were Er, Onan, Shelah, Perez and Zerah, though Er and Onan had died in the land of Canaan. The sons of Perez were Hezron and Hamul. Issachar’s sons were Tola, Puvah, Iob and Shimron. Zebulun’s sons were Sered, Elon and Jahleel. These are Leah’s sons, born to Jacob in Paddan-aram, with his daughter Dinah. Counting sons and daughters, this branch of the family came to thirty-three people. Gad’s sons were Ziphion, Haggi, Shuni, Ezbon, Eri, Arodi and Areli. Asher’s sons were Imnah, Ishvah, Ishvi and Beriah, and they had a sister, Serah. Beriah’s sons were Heber and Malkiel. These were the descendants of Zilpah, whom Laban had given to his daughter Leah. She bore these to Jacob, sixteen persons in all. The sons of Jacob’s wife Rachel were Joseph and Benjamin. In Egypt, Joseph had two sons, Manasseh and Ephraim. Their mother was Asenath, daughter of Potiphera, priest of On. Benjamin’s sons were Bela, Becher, Ashbel, Gera, Naaman, Ehi, Rosh, Muppim, Huppim and Ard. These were Rachel’s descendants born to Jacob, fourteen people in all. Dan’s son was Hushim. Naphtali’s sons were Jahzeel, Guni, Jezer and Shillem. These were the descendants of Bilhah, whom Laban had given to his daughter Rachel. She bore these to Jacob, seven persons in all. Jacob’s own descendants who traveled with him to Egypt came to sixty-six, without counting his sons’ wives. Joseph had two sons who were born to him in Egypt. So the whole household of Jacob that came to Egypt numbered seventy.

Jacob meets Joseph again

Jacob had Judah go ahead of him to Joseph, so that Joseph could show the way to Goshen. And they came into the land of Goshen. Joseph got his chariot ready and went up to Goshen to meet his father Israel. The moment he came before his father, he flung his arms around his neck and wept, and went on weeping a long while. Israel said to Joseph, “Now let death come. I have looked on your face, and I know you are alive.” Joseph said to his brothers and to the rest of his father’s family, “I am going up to Pharaoh to give him the news. I will tell him, ‘My brothers and my father’s family, who were living in Canaan, have arrived to join me. These men are shepherds, people who have kept livestock all along, and they have come with their sheep and goats, their cattle and all their belongings.’ When Pharaoh summons you and asks what you do for a living, answer, ‘We your servants have kept livestock since we were young, and so did our fathers before us.’ That way you will be able to live in the land of Goshen, because Egyptians loathe everyone who herds sheep.”

fields.title: Genesis 47
fields.body_html:
Jacob’s family in Goshen, and the famine in Egypt

Joseph went in to Pharaoh with the news. “My father and brothers have come from Canaan with their sheep and goats, their cattle, and all they own. At this moment they are in the land of Goshen.” He had brought five of his brothers with him, and he presented them to Pharaoh. Pharaoh asked Joseph’s brothers, “What do you do?” They replied, “Your servants keep flocks, as our fathers did before us.” They went on, “We have come to live in this country as foreigners for a while. The famine weighs hard on Canaan, and there is no pasture left there for the flocks your servants keep. Now please let your servants make their home in the land of Goshen.” Then Pharaoh said to Joseph, “Your father and your brothers have come to you. The whole land of Egypt is open to you. Give your father and brothers a home in the best part of the country; they may live in Goshen. And if there are capable men among them that you know of, make them chief herdsmen over the livestock that is mine.” Joseph then brought in his father Jacob and had him stand before Pharaoh, and Jacob gave Pharaoh his blessing. Pharaoh asked Jacob, “How many years have you lived?” Jacob replied, “I have lived as a foreigner for 130 years. My years have been few and hard, and they fall short of the years my fathers lived as foreigners.” Jacob blessed Pharaoh again as he took his leave. Joseph gave his father and brothers a home in Egypt, granting them land of their own in the finest part of the country, the region of Rameses, just as Pharaoh had said. Joseph fed his father, his brothers and all his father’s household, giving each family food in proportion to its little ones. Food was gone from the whole land, so cruel had the famine become, and both Egypt and Canaan grew faint under it. As people bought grain, Joseph took in all the money there was in Egypt and in Canaan, and he deposited it in Pharaoh’s palace. When the money in Egypt and Canaan ran out, the Egyptians all came to Joseph. “Give us food,” they pleaded. “Must we die in front of you? We have no money left.” “If your money is used up,” Joseph answered, “hand over your livestock, and I will give you food in return for them.” The people led their animals to Joseph, and he traded them food for horses, for sheep and goats, for cattle and for donkeys. Through that whole year he sustained them with food, taking all their livestock in return. That year came to an end, and in the next they came to him again. “My lord,” they said, “we will not pretend otherwise: the money is spent, and the animals are already yours. We have nothing left to offer my lord but ourselves and our land. Why let us die before your eyes, our land as well as ourselves? Purchase us and our land in return for food. We will be Pharaoh’s slaves and our land will be his. Give us seed, so that we can live and not die, and the soil will not go to ruin.” So Joseph acquired all the farmland of Egypt for Pharaoh. The famine pressed so hard on the Egyptians that every one of them sold his field, and the land passed to Pharaoh. The people he relocated to the cities, throughout Egypt from border to border. Only the priests’ land he did not buy, because the priests had a fixed share of food from Pharaoh and lived on what Pharaoh allotted them. So they kept their land. Joseph told the people, “As of today, you and your land belong to Pharaoh; I have bought them for him. Here is seed. Go and sow your fields. At harvest time you will hand over one fifth to Pharaoh. Four parts out of five will be yours to use as seed for the fields and to feed yourselves, everyone in your homes and your little ones.” They replied, “You have kept us alive! Let us find favor with you, my lord, and we will be Pharaoh’s slaves.” Joseph laid this down as a rule for the land of Egypt, and it holds to this day: Pharaoh receives a fifth. The priests’ land was the only land that never came to belong to Pharaoh. Israel made its home in Egypt, in the land of Goshen. They gained land there, were fruitful, and multiplied greatly. Jacob lived on in Egypt for seventeen more years; his whole life came to 147 years. When Israel’s death was near, he summoned his son Joseph. “If you hold me in your favor,” he said, “put your hand under my thigh and pledge me your loyalty and faithfulness. Do not bury me in Egypt. When I lie down with my fathers, take me up out of Egypt and lay me in their grave.” “I will do what you have asked,” Joseph said. “Swear it to me,” Israel said, and Joseph swore it. Then Israel bowed down at the head of his bed.

fields.title: Genesis 48
fields.body_html:
Jacob blesses Ephraim and Manasseh

After these events, word came to Joseph that his father was sick, and he went, bringing his two sons, Manasseh and Ephraim. Jacob heard that his son Joseph had come to him, and Israel pulled himself together and sat up on his bed. Jacob said to Joseph, “At Luz, in the land of Canaan, God Almighty appeared to me and blessed me. He said to me, ‘I am about to make you bear fruit and grow many; I will form an assembly of peoples from you, and I will give this land to your descendants after you, to hold as their own for all time.’ So your two sons, who were born to you in Egypt before I came to join you, are now mine. Ephraim and Manasseh will count as my sons, no less than Reuben and Simeon. The children you have after them will belong to you; when the inheritance is shared out, they will be counted under their brothers’ names. As for me, when I was coming back from Paddan, Rachel died on me in the land of Canaan, on the road, while we were still some way from Ephrath, and I buried her there by the road that leads to Ephrath” (that is, Bethlehem). Israel caught sight of Joseph’s sons and said, “Who are these?” “These are my sons,” Joseph told his father, “the ones God has given me in this place.” Jacob said, “Bring them here to me, please, and I will bless them.” Age had dimmed Israel’s eyes, and he could not see. Joseph led the boys up to him, and he kissed them and held them in his arms. Israel said to Joseph, “I had given up hope of ever seeing your face, and look, God has shown me your children as well.” Joseph then moved the boys from beside his father’s knees, and he bowed low with his face to the ground. Joseph set the two of them before his father: Ephraim, held in his right hand, at Israel’s left, and Manasseh, held in his left hand, at Israel’s right. Then he brought them up close to him. Israel, though, stretched out his right hand and set it on the head of Ephraim, the younger boy, and his left hand on Manasseh’s head. He crossed his hands knowingly, for Manasseh was the firstborn. Then he blessed Joseph: “May the God in whose presence my fathers Abraham and Isaac lived, the God who has tended me like a shepherd from my birth until today, the angel who has rescued me from every harm, bless these boys. Through them may my name be remembered, and the names of my fathers Abraham and Isaac; and may they teem and grow many on the earth.” Joseph saw that his father had laid his right hand on Ephraim’s head, and he did not like it. He took his father’s hand, meaning to shift it off Ephraim’s head and onto Manasseh’s. Joseph said to his father, “Not like that, my father! The firstborn is this one. Your right hand belongs on his head.” But his father would not do it. “I know, my son, I know,” he said. “Manasseh’s line will also become a people, and it will be great as well. But his younger brother will rise higher still, and his descendants will fill whole nations.” On that day he blessed them, saying, “Israel will use your name when they bless, saying, ‘May God make you like Ephraim and Manasseh.’” In this way he set Ephraim before Manasseh. Israel went on, speaking to Joseph: “My death is near. But God will be with you all and will lead you back to your ancestors’ land. And to you, more than to your brothers, I give one mountain slope, Shechem, the one I took from the Amorites by my sword and my bow.”

fields.title: Genesis 49
fields.body_html:
Jacob’s last words to his sons

Jacob summoned his sons and said, “Come together, and I will tell you what lies ahead for you in the time to come.” “Come together and hear, you sons of Jacob; give ear to Israel your father. Reuben, my firstborn, you are my strength, the first child of my vigor, standing above the rest in honor, above the rest in power. Wild as surging water, you will not hold first place, for you mounted your father’s bed. Then you defiled it: he climbed onto my couch!

Simeon and Levi are brothers indeed; violence is what their blades are made for. May I never take part in their secret plans, and may my honor stay far from their gatherings. In their rage they murdered men, and for their own pleasure they lamed oxen. Their anger is fierce and their rage is merciless; may both be cursed! I will break them apart among Jacob and spread them out across Israel.

Judah, you are the one your brothers will praise. Your hand will grip your enemies by the neck; the sons of your father will bow low before you. Judah is a young lion; my son, you have come up from the kill. He crouches and stretches out like a lion, like a lioness: who would risk waking him? The scepter will not pass from Judah, nor the staff of command from between his feet, until its rightful owner comes; the peoples will obey him. He will tie his donkey to the vine, the colt of his donkey to the best of the vines; he will launder his clothes in wine, his robe in the blood of grapes. His eyes will be dark with wine, his teeth white with milk.

Zebulun will make his home where the sea meets the land; he will be a landing place for ships, his territory stretching toward Sidon.

Issachar is a strong-boned donkey, stretched out between the sheepfolds. He found that rest was good and the land delightful, so he stooped to carry loads and was put to forced labor.

Dan will win justice for his people, a tribe of Israel like the rest. May Dan be a snake on the road, a horned viper beside the path, that strikes at a horse’s heels and throws its rider off backward. For your salvation I wait in hope, LORD. Gad: a raiding band will press him hard, but he will turn and press at their heels.

Out of Asher will come rich food; he will furnish fine fare for a king.

Naphtali is a deer running free that speaks lovely words.

Joseph is a fruit-bearing branch, a fruit-bearing branch beside a spring, its shoots spilling over the wall. Archers made his life bitter; they shot at him and hounded him with hatred. Yet his bow did not waver, and his arms were kept nimble by the hands of the Mighty One of Jacob; from there, from the Shepherd, the Stone of Israel, from the God of your father, who will help you, and by the Almighty, who will bless you with blessings that fall from the sky above, blessings that rise from the deep lying below, blessings of breast and womb. The blessings your father gives are stronger than the blessings of my forebears, as far as the farthest of the ancient hills. Let them come down on Joseph’s head, on the crown of the one marked out from his brothers.

Benjamin is a wolf that tears its prey: in the morning he feeds on the kill, by evening he is sharing out the spoils.” Together these make up the twelve tribes of Israel. These are the words their father spoke over them when he blessed them; to each he gave a blessing of his own. Then he charged them: “I am soon to be gathered to my people. Lay me to rest with my fathers in the cave that lies in the field of Ephron the Hittite, the cave in the Machpelah field, east of Mamre in the land of Canaan, which Abraham bought, field and all, from Ephron the Hittite to own as a burial site. That is where Abraham was laid to rest with his wife Sarah, and Isaac with his wife Rebekah; and I laid Leah there too. The field with its cave was a purchase from the Hittites.” Jacob finished charging his sons. Then he lifted his feet back onto the bed, took his last breath, and was gathered to his people.

fields.title: Genesis 50
fields.body_html:
The burial of Jacob, and the death of Joseph

Joseph flung himself down on his father’s face, kissing him and weeping over him. Joseph instructed the physicians who served him to embalm his father, and so the physicians embalmed Israel. Forty days were needed for this, since embalming takes that long, and the Egyptians wept for him seventy days. Once the days of weeping for him had passed, Joseph addressed the household of Pharaoh: “If you look on me with favor, please speak for me in Pharaoh’s hearing and tell him: ‘My father bound me by an oath, saying, “I am about to die. Bury me in the grave I prepared for myself in the land of Canaan.” So now, please let me travel up there to bury my father; afterward I will return.’” “Go up and bury your father,” Pharaoh replied, “as you swore to him you would.” Joseph went up to bury his father, and with him went all Pharaoh’s officials, the senior men of his household and every leading man in Egypt, and also Joseph’s whole household, his brothers, and the household of his father. They left nothing in the land of Goshen but their little ones, their flocks and their herds. Chariots and riders went up with him as well, so that the camp was very large indeed. They came to Atad’s threshing floor, beyond the Jordan, and there they wailed long and bitterly; Joseph held seven days of mourning for his father. The people of the land, the Canaanites, watched the mourning at Atad’s threshing floor and said, “How bitterly the Egyptians are mourning!” So the place was given the name Abel-mizraim; it lies beyond the Jordan. So Jacob’s sons carried out for him exactly what he had instructed them. They bore him to the land of Canaan and laid him in the cave of the Machpelah field, east of Mamre, the field that Abraham had purchased from Ephron the Hittite to own as a burial site. Once his father was buried, Joseph returned to Egypt, he and his brothers and all who had gone up with him to bury his father. With their father dead, Joseph’s brothers began to worry. “Joseph may be nursing a grudge against us,” they said, “and he may pay us back in full for all the harm we did him.” So they had someone take a message to Joseph: “Your father, before he died, gave this order: ‘Say this to Joseph: “I beg you, forgive your brothers’ crime and their sin, the wrong they did to you.”‘ So now, please forgive the crime of the servants of your father’s God.” At their words Joseph wept. His brothers then came themselves and fell down before him, saying, “Here we are, your slaves.” Joseph answered them, “Have no fear. Do I stand in the place of God? Evil was what you planned against me; good was what God planned by it, so as to bring about what you see today: the lives of a great many people saved. So there is no need to fear. I will see that you and your little ones have what you need.” He comforted them, speaking kindly to them. Joseph went on living in Egypt together with his father’s household, and he reached the age of 110. Joseph saw Ephraim’s descendants to the third generation; the children of Machir, Manasseh’s son, were also received on Joseph’s knees at their birth. Joseph said to his brothers, “I am about to die, but God will not fail to come and help you; he will lead you up out of this land to the land he swore to give to Abraham, to Isaac and to Jacob.” Joseph then put the sons of Israel under oath: “God will not fail to come and help you, and when he does, you are to take my bones up with you from here.” Joseph died at 110 years of age. He was embalmed and put in a coffin in Egypt.

fields.title: Conclusion
fields.body_html:
Joseph died at 110 years of age. He was embalmed and put in a coffin in Egypt.

— Genesis 50:26

Genesis does not end with a wedding or a victory. It ends with a coffin. The book that opened with God breathing life into dust closes with Joseph’s body embalmed and laid in a box in a foreign country. It is an honest last sentence, but not a hopeless one, because of what Joseph said just before it.

The question the book leaves with you

Joseph’s family is safe and fed in Egypt, but it is not home, and the land they were promised belongs to others. Abraham owned only a field with a burial cave in it. Isaac and Jacob lived there as foreigners; old Jacob told Pharaoh, “My years have been few and hard.” After three generations, the great nation is seventy people living on someone else’s land. And yet Joseph’s last words are not about Egypt at all:

Joseph said to his brothers, “I am about to die, but God will not fail to come and help you; he will lead you up out of this land to the land he swore to give to Abraham, to Isaac and to Jacob.”

— Genesis 50:24

He makes his brothers swear to carry his bones with them. Joseph, who had more of Egypt than anyone, wanted to be buried in a promise. That is the question Genesis leaves with every reader: what will you trust when the promise has not yet arrived? Abraham trusted it when it seemed impossible; Joseph held to it in a pit, a prison and a palace, and at the last staked his body on it.

The letter to the Hebrews says of all of them that they died still holding to faith, not having received what was promised: “they saw it from far off and welcomed it.” Abraham, it says, “was waiting for the city with firm foundations, a city planned and built by God.”

Where the story goes next

The very next book opens with Jacob’s family multiplying in Egypt until a new king comes to the throne, “one who had never heard of Joseph”, and makes them slaves. When they cry out, Exodus says, “God remembered his covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.” Generations later, when Moses led the people out, he took Joseph’s bones with him, and they were buried at last at Shechem, in the land.

But the promise to Abraham was larger than a land. It was that “all the families of the earth” would be blessed through him, and the New Testament says plainly where that came true. Paul writes to the Galatians:

“Scripture saw in advance that God would justify the Gentiles by faith, and so it announced the gospel ahead of time to Abraham: ‘In you all the nations will be blessed.’”

— Galatians 3:8

The offspring of the woman who would strike the serpent’s head, the descendant of Abraham through whom the nations would be blessed, the ruler from Judah who would hold the scepter: the New Testament gathers all these threads into Jesus Christ. And the promise now belongs to everyone who trusts him: “if you belong to Christ, it follows that you are Abraham’s offspring, heirs in keeping with the promise.”

Where to go from here

Genesis has been preached for as long as there has been a church, and some of the best of that work is in this library. A few places to begin:

  • On creation (Genesis 1). Basil of Caesarea’s The Hexaemeron, nine homilies on the six days; the closing books of Augustine’s Confessions, on time and eternity and the opening words of Genesis; and the second book of Theophilus of Antioch’s To Autolycus, on the prophets and the creation.
  • On the fall and its long shadow (Genesis 3–11). John Milton’s Paradise Lost, the English epic of the fall; and Augustine’s The City of God, whose books XI–XVI trace the two cities from the creation and the fall, through Cain and Abel and the flood, to Abraham and beyond.
  • On Enoch and Noah (Genesis 5–7). George Whitefield’s sermon Walking with God (Genesis 5:24) and D. L. Moody’s Come Thou and All Thy House into the Ark (Genesis 7:1).
  • On Abraham. Alexander Maclaren’s Jehovah-Jireh (Genesis 22:14), and his The Gift That Brings All Gifts, which hears Abraham and Isaac behind Romans 8:32; E. M. Bounds’s Prayer and Praying Men, with its chapter on Abraham, the man of prayer; and William J. Seymour’s Rebecca: Type of the Bride of Christ (Genesis 24).
  • On the faith of the patriarchs. Jonathan Edwards’s The Christian Pilgrim, on Hebrews 11:13–14 and the patriarchs who called themselves strangers on the earth; Gareth Evans’s He Holds My Tomorrows, which walks through the faith of Hebrews 11 from Abel onward; and The Prayers Jesus Learned, an Ochorus Original that begins with Abraham pleading for a city and Jacob wrestling through the night.
  • On the covenant. Andrew Murray’s The Two Covenants, which begins its comparison of the old covenant and the new in Abraham’s household; and Charles H. Spurgeon’s The Blood of the Everlasting Covenant.

You can also go the other way, from the text to the classics. Every reference to Genesis in this library can be tapped to read the verse, and the Scripture pages gather, chapter by chapter, what the great writers of the church have said about each passage of this book.

And then read on, for Genesis is the first chapter of a story not finished on its last page. It begins with a God who walks in a garden and asks a hiding man a question, and the question has not gone away:

But the LORD God called to the man, “Where are you?”

— Genesis 3:9
